title: Dave Canales on rookie minicamp Day 2 takeaways | Carolina Panthers
text: All right, first of all, early happy Mother's Day to all the mothers out there. Uh grateful um you know, uh a group of men doing what we get to do. Uh it's a great time for us to be able to celebrate that and and be so thankful and grateful for all the hard work, the love, support, the Gatorades, the cleats, um all the things that come with it. And so, uh happy Mother's Day there. And we'll open up for questions. Any takeaways specifically, Dave, about Monroe's two days here, whether it's in a meeting or something he did out here? >> I mean, first of all, he looks great. Um, he's been, uh, he's been working really hard. Just just trying to continue to, you know, uh, increase his strength and do those things. Um, showed up, I think he was, you know, about 325. Um, and, uh, looked great, moved well, um, showed the length and all the things. and you know, he's just got to get comfortable with some of our schemes and concepts, playing next to a tight end who might be blocking front side and going backside and, uh, settling into some of those things. But, um, looks like a guy that really enjoys football. Those are the types of guys that we love to have here. >> 25's a little bigger than he played at, I think, was that something that you guys talked about maybe him getting a little bigger. >> Not really. That was just kind of an emphasis of his. And I mean, if you think the guy's 21 years old, you know, so, um, he's still growing into whatever his frame is. And um I think he played somewhere in the 310sish or something like that, 315 during the season, but as we know, seasons get long and guys have a chance to kind of settle in and focus on some things and and the work showed up. But he he looks great. He's moving well. So really pleased with that. >> Do you almost have to make an allowance for guys out here during this camp because most of these dudes have been in combine training or pre-draft different kind of not football? >> Abs. Absolutely. Uh that's something we have to be really aware of as we come into these camps where um you know the guys are working out, they're they're practicing drills that they go through at pro days or the combine. Um and those drills are pretty set, you know, but once you're starting to react to movement and you get back to playing a little bit of football, um that does work different parts of your body. And so, you know, postdraft they really have two weeks, some guys a week before they hit rookie mini camp. We always do it on the second uh second weekend after the draft, you know, to hopefully give those guys a chance to, you know, get their cleats on and just kind of settle into their normal type of football training. >> Two days outside >> with Haynes King. What has stood out to you about him? >> Yeah. Um, you know, first of all, off the film, the thing I was most excited about is you just watch his offense move the chains. Third and fourth down, two-minute drill, the ball goes down the field, they score points. Um, and there's a bunch of ways you can affect the game as a quarterback with your mind, with your arm, and with your legs. And he's got a way that he's able to find wins that way. Uh, it was great to see him in person. Um, just, you know, work around coming off play actions. Um, the bootlegs. Um, and then just certainly seeing the athleticism that he has in his body show up through his arm. A lot of zip, a lot of pop there. and and a guy that really was um he did a great job in the classroom also just making sure like these camps only go as well as a quarterback's ability to operate get them out of the out of the huddle to the line of scrimmage with a cadence. I think we might have had two pre- snap penalties in two days. That's pretty rare for a rookie mini camp. And so I got to attribute that attribute that to Rashad and also to Haynes for operating that way. And um Brad has spent a lot of time with the quarterbacks particularly today. Um is that a function of him just calling the offense in rookie mini camp or is that um is there something more there? No, that's been something that Brad's been doing for for the last couple of years since we've been here is trying to make sure that he he's got a lot of familiarity with the wide receiver play, but getting into the quarterback room um especially now, you know, calling plays and and being in in really in charge of the offense, putting the implementation of it, just to make sure that the language is on the same page and the intent of what we're trying to do is there, but also just a growth opportunity for Brad to continue to press into uh the training of a quarterback. And uh that's something that I had great mentors that taught me and something that I' I've loved to be able to have conversations with for Brad to continue to, you know, look at the whole group and be able to uh impact it that way. >> We've heard you talk a lot about the the kind of mental side of things for the center position. What has uh what's been your takeaway on Sam from that regard? >> Yeah, Sam's handled this in stride. Um he's done a great job in these last couple of days. Excited to throw more on his plate as we get back together with the full group. But, um, again, what showed up for Sam is on film, you see a guy that's under control, a guy that, uh, plays the center position really well. Um, you know, at a professional level, even from his film last year. And that's what showed up in these last two days is, you know, the his ability to stay calm, make the point, work his combos with the guys, um, and just kind of bring that that type of balance and cohesiveness that you need to have with the inside three. Coach Chris Bazard uh after the draft selection, one of the talking heads um says it's a great pick for if he holds it all together, indicating that there's some kind of lack of potential there. Um he comes from an athletic family. I'm sorry, but there's a one arrest that he had regarding driver's license, but other than that, there was nothing else. >> Chris has done a great job. He's uh he loves playing. He loves working on his craft. Um we that kind of emerged in the process as we were talking to him as a guy that loves to get out there and work his footwork and do different things and um you know I have a friend who actually coaches in the area um that has had exposure with Chris before you know and has worked with him on the field and so um the whole process gave us confidence in this guy um being able to just continue to have the uh the foundation to build his skills to build all the the tools that he needs because he's really into it. um that's what we're mostly concerned with and uh you know as far as like the last couple of days he's done a great job pressing into it but as you can imagine I think we talked about this yesterday you know this is different you know we have all these different splits and where we put guys in stacks and um are you inside or outside the numbers and all those things those are going to be the things that Chris is going to really need to dive into. >> You do put a lot of emphasis obviously on character. Were there any questions with him that you wanted to have answered? >> Not at all. I think it was just a matter of us getting to know the guy and and how he learns um how he relates from a personal standpoint and we did the work. You know, we we had him in the uh at the combine in the formal meetings. Uh we brought him in for a 30 visit. We followed up with Zooms. Um just to check all those boxes of this is a guy that we would love to work with because the football skills and you know the speed, the ability to track the ball down the field at his height to be able to drop his weight, get in and out of breaks, it's rare. and uh we were just really really excited u that we were able to just stay put where we were at and he came to us in the third round and um so excited for to see what happens when he gets with the rest of the guys. >> How important are reps like this for a guy like Justine Reed and you know what have you what have you seen from the wide receiver? >> Justine's done a great job for us since we got him here. Um you know we have a little bit of a commonality. He went to University of San Diego. That was our opening day at ISUsa Pacific way back when. So, um, but anyway, speaking to like what he's doing now, getting to this camp, um, to really show us what he knows and also, uh, the training that he's gotten from Rob, um, it really shows up and and when you get a a new group of wide receivers out there, it's good to have someone like Jim out there with them where they can kind of see this is how we want this route run. This is how we want this drill done. He did a great job these couple of days. >> Coach, >> sorry. >> Paint is an older guy. When you when you get a guy like that that's been in college for a while, which has kind of become the norm the last couple years, how much of a difference can you tell when you get them out here for the first? >> There certainly is. Um, for the guys that we're seeing, you know, 24 and 25 year olds coming out and there's a maturity to them. Uh, there's a professionalism about how they u handle their life inside the building and outside of the building. Just kind of having their world in order. Um, Haynes gives that feel, you know, like he's he's a pro, you know, me mentally speaking. And now the challenge is how quickly can we get him caught up in all of our schemes, concepts, protections, all the different things at the line of scrimmage and and right now he's pouring himself into it, doing a great job. >> Dave, the nickel position seems like something that you're very much open competition with. Devonte Smith has plenty of playing time at the college level. I don't know if you've watched all the film from him yesterday, but what stood out to you about him? >> Yeah, versatility. Uh spent a lot of time in the slot playing the nickel, but a guy that can certainly play outside, too. So, um it's a good group. you know, Will Lee, uh, the length, you see that too as well. Um, these guys are, you know, that position right there. We have Shaw coming back. We have Corey Thornton, um, who really, you know, won the job during the season last year and got an opportunity till he got hurt. So, there's a great competition already happening. We love to throw more more possible guys at each position. Uh, competition just breeds success. It breeds growth, development, and um, guys really start to push each other. So, I'm excited to to get those guys with the full group. Coach Brad is getting like the sort of level of energy that the rest of receivers are out there. You know, how important is the maxi energy of the players out there as coaches? >> Yeah, we set the tone. You know, that's a reminder for us. It's our sixth day in a row on the field and uh we got to treat it like it's our first and bring that same intentionality uh the intensity to the individual drills and uh making sure we're pushing these guys so they can understand what the expectation is of how we practice. And so really critical uh that the players they got their own energy that they come into with this excitement of this opportunity and the competition, but as coaches um we have to just make sure that that stays at a fever pitch so that we have great speed. Uh that's the best way you learn is is we can push the guys and and also just to enjoy what we're doing. You know, we get to come out here on the grass and coach football one more day and um that part I know the the players will look at us and they see us excited about it. They'll they'll maintain that energy. >> All right. Thank you very much. >> All right. Thank you. Yeah.

I mean it's it's a it's a way to just get them acclimated with what we're going to do schematically, what we're going to ask him to do physically, you know, so that they get ready in a week. Is that a Is that a fair assessment? I mean, the the from a protection standpoint, um he's obviously physically a very good protector. Now we got to teach him the scheme of it. Uh his it that his demeanor, I guess you could say, but it I that hasn't really stood out. I'm not I'm not shocked. Um he loves it. He loves just sitting there. I wanted him to be with Shab and and Hackett a lot, so I stood there for about 10 minutes. And usually I just mess stuff up anyways in terms of talking about, you know, God knows what. So, but no, it's it's kind of what I expected. With Carson, [snorts] is it kind of nice to have a a quarterback that was drafted in the third round just because you can kind of let him develop at his own pace without having the pressure of being a first-round pick, you know, that is supposed to be impact right away? I'm not going to sit here and, you know, lie and say, "Hey, the first round's different than the seventh round." title: QB Carson Beck Introductory Press Conference | Arizona Cardinals 2026
text: Now that you're here, what's it what's it been like these last hour or so just being on campus and kind of seeing everything? >> Yeah, it's been super cool. Um, obviously from Jacksonville, Florida, so far ways away on the other side of the US. You know, getting to come out to the West Coast essentially is somewhere that, you know, I've never lived. I've really have only been here a couple of times. Obviously, we played out here in the Fiesta Bowl, uh, you know, a couple months ago, but I'm really excited to be here. Michael Flores has said that if you outplay the other guys, you have a chance to see the field early in the season. How does that shape your approach, especially during, you know, OTA's mini camp, training camp what? >> Yeah, I think for me, uh, the most important thing is a get in the building. Um, you know, I started meeting with the coaches and going over the playbook and, you know, learn the guys around me, build relationships, start to connect with them, be myself, and then just go play ball, you know, have fun, enjoy the process. Um, but again, just try to improve and get better each and every day. Um, and if I continue to do that, I think we'll see, you know, where that takes me. >> Obviously, that's a learning the playbook is is particularly crucial for a quarterback. Where where do you feel like you're at in in that process? And how much of it do you have down so far? >> Yeah, I mean, it's literally been like a week or two of like, you know, going through it and learning the lingo and the concepts and, you know, the reads and the footwork and, you know, just the whole process of that. Um, and again, that's that the playbook's huge, right? Which again, I've kind of had the um the luxury of being in two different systems that have done a lot of different things at Georgia, at Miami. Um, and football's football at the end of the day. You know, the concepts are going to be the concepts, but you know, just talking with coach Hackett, talking with Coach SH, you know, going through the playbook and seeing how they see the game. It's it's it's been really cool, and I I've really been able to learn a lot even in these first couple of weeks. Much has been much has been made about your experience. I'm wondering where you think that shows up the most for you. Is it this part where you're like learning the playbook and you've been through so much of it? Is it going to be actually on the field? Where do you think the experience shows up the most? >> Yeah, I mean I think the experience obviously helps in a multitude of ways. um when it comes to being on the field, when it comes to, you know, picking up a playbook uh faster. Uh having to learn the Miami playbook, I think kind of prepared me for this a little bit. Uh obviously, Georgia was my kind of baseline knowledge. I was there for 5 years. I I knew the playbook like the back of my hand. You know, obviously, I'm sure they've changed the lingo a little bit compared to what it was when I was there, but I mean, we could go back there and I could tell you every formation, played, route, concept, protection, even this point, you know, two years out of it. Um, so again, but the experience is nothing if there's no, you know, application from the lessons that you've learned from the experiences. So again, if you know, I can continue to apply the lessons I've learned from those experiences, I think it can help in a multitude of ways. >> I know you can't give away the whole playbook right now, but what elements of this offensive system and this playbook do you feel like will suit your strengths? >> Yeah. Um, you know, I think something that again I've been a part of, uh, in the past with being in the Georgia offense, uh, with coach Bobo and then, uh, Coach Dawson at Miami is there's a lot of, you know, peer progressions and you're reading across the field and it's not just pick a side, pick a side, right? Obviously, you have every single different, you know, play action and pure progression and full field read across the board. All these different reads and progressions that you can make, but you know, I think that's something that I've been really comfortable with uh throughout my college career and uh is something that obviously gets translated at this level as well. >> That was obviously a big discussion in the fall around NFL quarterbacks talking about pure progression versus uh you know, reading the field. Why why do you like pure progression? Why why do you feel like that suits you? Yeah, I think it just always gives you answers uh based off of uh what the defense is doing and obviously in today's day and age, you know, defenses are getting better and better and disguising things and obviously I mean there's athletes all over the field, right? The the margins get smaller and smaller and especially at this level um what it takes to win a football game, right? Uh again to have as many options available on each and every play to give you the you know highest percentage of success and to move the ball down the field is always important and again that's that's kind of where the baseline starts of it. >> When you were on uh Gruden's QB class, one of the viral clips was him talking with you about the snap count. Obviously the clap is not a thing uh in the NFL. So what kind of goes into actually developing that convincing snap count? >> Yeah. Um, actually this past year at Miami for the the first half of the season, we actually did like a verbal cadence. It it obviously isn't as drawn out as, you know, the the cadences in the league and how many different variants and um ways you can try to trick a defense or just kind of keep them off balance. You know, you can use cadence as a weapon. Uh, so obviously that's something that I'm going to have to practice as, you know, I head into this, but I think it'll be good and like I said, you can use that as a weapon if you can get good at it. So, I'm I'm excited to, you know, kind of dive into that a little bit more >> with uh with the different situations you've been in in terms of the quarterback room going into a season. Uh and obviously the the veterans on this team are going to have a leg up just because of their experience and stuff, but have you been through a a an an openish competition like this? Sounds like it's going to be at least that's what Monty has talked about. Um, I mean, I guess the the first year that I would have started at Georgia, which would have been what, um, 2023, um, right after Stson had left, I mean, that was an open competition. And, um, again, whether you're the the fourth string guy, the the starter, it's it's important that you approach each and every day the exact same. And, you know, you exude energy and, um, and you bring it. You know, you be yourself each and every day. And you know, that's kind of what I've always tried to stand for, you know, in in my college career. So, I I hope to continue to bring that and be myself and compete and um we'll see where that takes me. >> Where do you stand on wanting to kind of sit and learn and watch and absorb as much as you can your first year versus trying to if if the opportunity arose to play and kind of learn on the fly? >> Yeah, absolutely. Um I mean each and every day will be a learning experience even even you know if I you know were to be the guy at some point you are consistently and constantly learning just through game experience through pract experience um meetings every I mean just talking to guys around the facility right just trying to get all the little breadcrumbs that I can from each and every person uh but again uh everybody wants to play football especially at the position of quarterback you want to be the guy out there it's such a interesting position what why I think it's the best position on earth there's only one guy out there you know it's not wide receiver. If you're an 11 personnel, you got three guys out there. You know, Dline, you're you you're a four down team, you got four guys out there, right? At quarterback, there's one guy out there doing it. So, I mean, obviously, I would love to, you know, play and perform. Uh, but again, we we'll see where that u where that takes me and really just showing up and going to go to work. >> Coach Laflur said uh a couple times now, one of the things that made your possibility attractive to him was that you have been through some stuff. And I'm assuming that's some adversity or whatever. Do you feel like that gives you a leg up coming into the NFL that you've been through some stuff? >> Um, I think going through things and facing adversity obviously helps you if you respond to it the correct way. um just going through stuff doesn't you know give me a leg up necessarily on anybody if if I don't use that or um you know respond to it in the in the correct way and again yes I I have faced a lot of adversity and in my career it's never been perfect um there's been ups there's been downs there have been really good moments and there's also been really low moments um and all of that has kind of accumulated and created who I am today as a quarterback and as a person as well so again taking all those experiences and and ultimately applying them into where I'm at now with, you know, in a in a new place with fresh faces and new coaches and new players around me. Um, I'm obviously really excited and hopefully can can apply that. >> Who have been the most important people to kind of help you through those ups and downs across multiple schools and stuff? Who who have been the people that have made that possible for you? >> Yeah, absolutely. Uh, I mean, first and foremost to my teammates that, you know, I've had around me uh from Georgia to Miami. Um, I mean you I can't talk highly enough of the guys that have been around me that have, you know, stood there by my side when in amazing moments and in bad moments as well. You know, uh, those are guys you lean on. You're in the building with them each and every day. I mean, working hours and hours constantly. Um, and again, that's that's the grind of college football and and what you're doing, what you're what is expected of you. So again, th those teammates and then obviously the coaches uh that I've had that have always showed constant support for me and always had my back from the beginning. Um I'm obviously super thankful for the the two situations that I was able to be a part of and then obviously ultimately, you know, come into this. >> When you get to Miami, you were still injured, so you had to kind of like learn everyone's process and just get to know everyone without being on the field. What can you take from that experience to kind of help you kind of get into this locker room and kind of learn learn? >> Yeah, absolutely. Uh I think going through that process definitely helped. Um and I think heading into this process, obviously it's a new league and um it it will be different uh than than college of course, but you know going through that transition of learning a new team and uh being the the new guy on the block again. Obviously it's a little different being a transfer compared to you know being a a freshman, right? So, I I'm kind of the the freshman, per se, the the rookie in the in the building. Um, and again, you you come in, you you put your your hard hat on, and you go to work. Uh, that's that's what you do. That's that's how it's been. That's what I did at Miami. Obviously, it looked a little bit different because I couldn't practice. I couldn't throw a football. I I had to find ways to kind of um put myself into situations where I could build these relationships with the players. try to be a coach on the field is really the um the perspective and kind of what I did whenever I got there because I have a brace on my elbow you know so obviously this will be a little bit different because I will be able to be out on the field and you know practice and be with the guys and uh it'll it'll be good. No, I'm really excited and I do think that experience definitely you know will will help with this one. >> What's your first impression of this rookie class right now? The guys that you've met so far. >> Yeah, absolutely. Um, I mean, shoot, literally I just met them all in person for I mean the first time like two hours ago, but uh I mean shoot everyone everyone seems really cool. Uh some it seems like a lot of great guys and obviously over the the next um couple days especially we'll get to spend a lot of time together and then obviously over the course of the next couple weeks, months and you know so on and so forth I'll get to know them a little bit better. But I'm excited uh about the guys that are coming in. Obviously a lot of talent and seem like really good people. Were you ever concerned uh after the injury that it would never get back to the 100%? I mean, was there ever a time like that or was it just a question of it will be there? It's just I just got to give it time. >> Well, that's like the mental battle, you know, and and having an injury like that. And obviously at the quarterback position, that's probably the worst injury that you could possibly have. Um and again, it was the constant the mental battle back and forth of the two things that you just said. And you want to tell yourself always like it's going to be fine. and it's just going to take time. You just have to trust the process and you have a lot of really really good uh people around you that are going to help you, you know, get back to where you were. But then it's, you know, two months in and you still haven't thrown a football and you're sitting there and you're it's hard for you mentally. I say for you, but for myself, you know, being in that situation and um you know, just having to grind each and every day, uh again, it really gave me a new perspective. Um and really again, just realizing, man, like I just want to be out there. I want to play football like this. Like this sucks. You know, like it obviously was a really hard time for me and a difficult situation to go through, but again, I the guys at Miami really kind of rallied around me through that time and really helped me get through that from the trainers to the coaches to the teammates. So, >> was there a moment when you were like, "Yeah, I'm back." >> Um, so I went back up to Jacksonville in our uh which is where I'm from, from Jacksonville, Florida. And um it would have been during our discretionary period. So, I went up went back up there and had just started throwing again. And I mean, the first couple of days of throwing, it was like, oh my gosh. Like, I literally could only throw a ball like 10 yards, which is all I all I was allowed to. And I don't know if I could have thrown it farther if I had to. Um, but I think it was like two weeks in and they were they were talking, my guys up in Jacksonville were talking to me and they were like, "Just just let it rip. So that that would be that moment for sure. >> I saw Chris I said uh that you're he feels like you're just now at 100% and that your best football's ahead of you. I guess do you feel different with Diablo now compared to November from now to November when you when you last played in the competitive game I guess January would >> um I would I would say towards the the end of the season in the playoffs. I mean my arm felt great but it only continues to get stronger and now that I'm what a year and a half out of surgery. I mean my arm is the strongest it's ever been. Um, and I I feel like I've been throwing the ball really well recently. And then obviously finally having a an off season to train and work and lock in on, you know, mechanics and um just the fluidity of your motion and, you know, pairing everything together and um, you know, making sure the mechanics are 100% in exactly what I want them to be. Um, and again, I think that has also really helped, but again, you know, my my arm feels great. um it has for a while now, but I think really being able to hone in and have an offseason to train and focus on it compared to, you know, the year before where I have the surgery, I'm rehabbing, I'm trying to learn a new offense, it's you're really not able to focus on, you know, those kind of like small minute details. I think I think that has really helped, you know, being able to have this offseason. >> Was that a full-blown Tommy John surgery? >> Uh no, it was not it wasn't full-blown Tommy John. It was a um a repair. So full a full full-blown Tommy John would be a reconstruction of the UCL where obviously they take the tendon and reconstruct it. Uh mine did not tear in half. It ripped off the bone. Uh yeah, not fun. Uh [laughter] definitely did not enjoy that. Uh but so they they go back in uh they they repair it and you know it's it's a lot faster of a um a healing process compared to full-blown Tommy John. after the injury after the transfer, what do you think you showed either yourself or just everyone else as well taking Miami on that on that run? >> Um, I'd say resilience. Um, I I feel like just again having the the elbow injury. Um, you know, having to go to a new school where, you know, people doubted us and you look in that locker room of the talent that we had and I mean we're looking at each other like what I can't believe people are, you know, saying whatever they were saying about our team, right? because obviously we had a lot of belief in oursel and you know kind of knew what we were capable of. Uh just going out to work and um each and every day you look at the edges and you see Ruben Bane and Meador and that whole defense and then all the talent on offense as well and um again it it was an up and down season. Again it wasn't perfect. It never was but the resilience that that team showed um I definitely define that season with that word. It's your first time in a building here with the northeast obviously, but since the draft, has Jacobe, Gardner, any veterans reached out to you about what to expect or welcoming you in? >> Um, yeah. I mean, I've been able to, you know, talk to a couple of the guys on the team. Um, and obviously just meeting a lot of them uh for the first time uh today, right? Again, I've only been in this in the facility for maybe like two or three hours, which again, I'm I'm super excited and really until it's kind of now just hitting me that, you know, this is all real. I mean, it's it's very surreal for me. I'm obviously super excited and just continuing to meet the guys and obviously I'll get to know them a little bit better here over the next couple of weeks, but I'm I'm really excited for this opportunity. >> Harris mentioned that you guys took a official visit to Georgia together. Just what's it mean to team up with him now and some of the other offensive playmakers here? >> Yeah, absolutely. I mean, obviously he's been I mean, one of the most highly touted guys since high school. Um, yeah, we we did we took a visit together at Georgia. Really aged me a little bit. Uh [laughter] he he had reached out and texted me. Um and yeah, I was laughing about it, but no, it'll it'll be cool obviously to kind of reconnect with some of the guys that I've known in the past and obviously he's a a super talented player. >> There's so much pressure I think seems like on young athletes just to get to the next level so so quickly these days, your journey taking a little longer. Would you would you recommend that? Um, I I think everybody's got to, you know, run their own race and it it looks different for everyone regardless of the opinions that, you know, others have on that race or on that journey. Um, you know, I I sat for three years. I I always wanted to be the quarterback at the University of Georgia from the second that I committed there. And I was going to sit there and wait and work and make sure that I was prepared when that moment came. Um, then I was able to, you know, start there for two years and we won a ton of football games. We had a ton of talent on those teams and to get to play for um you know, coach Smart and do that and learn under one of the best college football coaches ever. Um you know, develop me as a player, develop me as a man and then I get the elbow, I go to Miami, I get to play for coach Crystal Ball who I mean the relationship that we built was I mean one to none. um the just the time and the effort that you know he put into our team, the intensity um the the mind, the knowledge of what he was able to do with our team and the talent and utilize that. Um I mean those three years that you know I had of playing and starting are priceless. Um and and really the the only way that you can gain that is by doing it. So again, everyone's [clears throat] got to run their race. Mine was obviously a little bit different where I did stay in college a little bit longer. That was obviously not the plan when I was 17, 18 years old going into college. I would have loved to start as a freshman, play three years, and get there as quick as possible. But, um, you know, I I do feel like, uh, you know, my process and the experiences I went through will will bode well for me in the future. >> You've been in the spotlight. >> Last one, guys. >> You've been in the spotlight for a couple years now. I'm playing at Miami, Georgia. Going through the the draft and stuff. There's a lot of things said about you and there will continue to be a lot of things said and written about you. Just are you a guy that bulletin board material? Do do you tune out the noise? like how do you operate whenever you see that kind of noise? >> Yeah. Um I don't know. I never really listen to it whether it's good or bad. Uh and and that's where I feel like a lot of guys mess up because they they won't listen to the bad but they'll listen to the good. But it's all poison. Um at the at the end of the day either they're, you know, fueling you up or they're tearing you down. And at the end of the day, the the only people's opinion that mattered are the the guys in the building, right? Your coaches, your teammates. Um what they're saying to you, what what they're teaching you, what they're coaching you. if you can lock in on that. And you know, that's really what I've done the past couple of years as I've continued to, you know, play more and more football. And again, it's it's worked out for me, um, you know, from a mental standpoint. So, again, I'll I'll stick to that.

text: What's uh what are your thoughts getting here for the first time? Uh I had a top-30 visit. It was fun and now being back for good is is a blessing for sure. I'm just excited. I know I'm I'm a great blocker for like my strength I know my strength it doesn't look like it, but I'm pretty strong, though. I know you said you said you've been improving your strength. Where would What other parts of your game would you like to improve? Um just being as big as I am, just in and out of my breaks. Um just after the catch, too. I've been working on that a lot. Um I've been working with guys like Mohamed Sanu and Mike Evans. We've been working on like my run after catch, and then I have my other trainers who help with that. It's just the the consistency of doing those little things right. So, just being around them, um just catching the ball in my eyes, like where I can use my hands, when I'm releasing, see where I'm where I'm shooting out shooting my hands at. Just being able to be smart, um reading defenses, and stuff like that. It's just the little things and making the fundamentals really sharp, so then you'll be good. title: Zachariah Branch & Kendal Daniels speak after the first day of rookie minicamp | Press Conference
text: how you feeling after first one first one done. >> I feel great. Um, you know, very blessed for the opportunity that the organization has given me. Um, you know, the coaches want to coach you on certain things. I like to get coached hard. Um, and I'm I'm kind of a perfectionist, so I don't like messing up. Uh, so I like to be on my details and things like that. So after I finish this, I plan on going over there and doing my jugs and just controlling the things I can like preparing and understanding the playbook and learning it from inside and outside so I can be able to be out there and take advantage of the opportunities I do get when I am on the field. >> From your perspective, from your perspective, maybe what's the hardest thing about being a rookie whether mentally or physically? I apologize from college to the NFL. Um you know it's a different level. How much do you kind of thrive with these opportunities to kind of show everybody to make them believes in what you can do? >> Oh, yes. Uh that's that's one of my main focuses just to be able to, you know, control what I can at the end of the day. So, when you do get the opportunity, um, you know, you're as ready as possible. So, that's pretty much my goal. >> Anything else? >> All right. Thanks, y'all. >> Appreciate you guys. Thank you. >> How did the first day go? >> Great. It was amazing to be able to get back out there. Like what were some of the emotions? >> Uh, I think it's sunk in a little bit, you know, being out there on the NFL field and and seeing um the NFL head coaches and everything, coach Definsky and um all those guys. But I don't know if it really set in yet. I think I'm just in the mode of learning plays and and just kind of in the grind right now, I think it'll set in once um I don't know, probably once training camp comes and the pads get back on. Probably when I meet the older guys and get out there with them. Um but I'm just enjoying the moment right now. >> How are the dorms? >> Great. They're they're amazing. Yeah, they they're kind of it reminded me I told my wife, it kind of reminded me when I first went to college. Um being away from her and and being in my own dorm room, just kind of just going in there and just watching film by myself in this quad. Yeah. Yeah. My boy Perk. >> You guys getting to know each other? >> Yeah, for sure. Yeah, we played against each other. We talked at the combine a lot. Um talked about the game we played against him. Do you feel like you have a good balance right now of having fun but also trying to like soak in all the information? How's that been? >> Yeah, it's been um I've been trying to dial it back because I talk a lot of uh smack, you know, probably in the middle of the season I'll be talking a little bit more just, you know, I'm used to talking to John here and all those guys. But it's fun being out there and being able to play and really learn the plays. Um it's fun though, you know, it's fun to be able to get my feet back in the grass and and learn the plays and feel the stress of trying not to mess up. Um that's fun. um after the fact that you've already done it, but it's been good. >> So, you say stress, you're not too overwhelmed with the amount of plays you're trying to learn right now. >> No, I I feel like I don't want to say I I'm prepared for it. But, Coach Vibable has probably prepared me the most. Um the first day I got there, there was 10 plays installed and and it was kind of like learn them or or don't play. So, it was kind of today was was smooth and just to get the details down and be able to go out there and play fast and physical. you played uh you know so many different positions uh in college. What do you think is your is your best role? And >> is there something that might surprise us? Some position that you might have played that might that might surprise us? >> Uh I don't know. You know, it's been I played a lot of positions and I've been in a lot of situations. So, it's kind of hard. I'm just a rookie. Um so, I don't know what I'll be best at or what I'm best at. Um you know, I played everywhere last season and wherever they want me to play this season, I'll play it. If they want me to go hold hold the kick one field goal, I'll go do it. So, whatever they want me to do, I'll do it to the best of my ability. >> We have anything else? >> Are there any linebackers that you may model your game after or um anybody you take inspiration from having made the transition from >> defensive backfield to to linebacker? Uh, I would say, um, I watched a lot of Devon's, uh, film, um, Diablo and, you know, seeing his how he transitioned and played in the defense is has really helped me because he came from the background and how he plays and how he moves around, you could just tell that he played safety and so knowing that somebody moved from safety to linebacker and this defense has helped me. Um, just watching his film and how calm, cool, and collected he is and and that has helped me just being able to watch his game and try to model my game a little bit, try to take pieces from other guys around the league. But it's been fun. >> What's your favorite part about your game? >> The favorite part about my game >> just as as a linebacker, as defensive player, athlete, whatever. Anything? >> I mean, that's hard. The favorite thing I like >> Yeah. >> Uh my versatility, just being able to be a plug-and-play linebacker. Um just the background or or whatever. And my the way I learn um I'm a fast learner. I say that and then I might come out tomorrow and bust out plug. I feel like I'm a fa fast learner and I learn quick and once I mess it up once I won't mess it up again hopefully. >> And do you see the comparisons kind of between what Jeff wants to do with this defense and what you did last year with Ben? >> Yeah. Yes. >> I know you mentioned your roommate with Perkins kind of knew him from the draft, but anyone else you know on this Falcons team? >> Um Billy. Um he reached out to me. He talked to me because we didn't play together, but I talked to him last year. He came to a couple of the practices and then when I got drafted he hit me up and AJ Terrell hit me up um and followed me on um and Jaylen Walker did too. It just it's crazy to see um it's just crazy that I'm in the NFL now and being uh in the same locker room as those guys. Um it's been um a lot but I'm taking it in well. >> Love it. Awesome. title: Head Coach Kevin Stefanski speaks ahead of the first practice at Rookie Minicamp | Atlanta Falcons
text: that AJ and Avon's family is experiencing. Uh you know, they put out their statements. I'm going to respect their privacy, but uh they know that myself, this entire organization is with them, uh through all this. So, uh just want to make sure um started with that with uh this weekend. Again, fun weekend for us to get our hands on our players. um a lot of young young men that are um walking in this room for the first time and walking into this building for the first time and going out there to practice. Just finished a walkthrough. So, a lot coming at them. They're drinking through the fire hose, but they're they're doing a nice job and their coaches are doing a nice job. So a lot of work to be done um and we're excited to get started with these young guys. With that I'll take any questions. What are the the main things that you look for on a weekend like this, Kevin? >> I think the for the players, their their goal here, uh, regardless of whether you're a draft pick, a undrafted free agent, a rookie try out, a veteran try out, your your goal is to learn our system and our systems when you include special teams. Get to know your teammates, get to know your coaches, uh, and then everything else will take care of itself. Uh uh truly, you know, this is really the first for the guys that are drafted and signed. This is their first experience in the building. They'll join the veterans on Monday uh in our phase two. So, really, we're trying to catch them up to speed as much as we can over the course of three days. >> Do you have any veteran scouts? >> We do. Yeah, we do. I don't have them off the top. >> Okay. And and Terrell, is he here? >> Yes. >> Kevin, what is your philosophy in general on playing rookies? And uh do you have a problem starting a rookie or do you prefer just kind of bring them along gradually? I >> I think uh in this day and age, we're counting on rookies to play in in this league oftent times. So there's no uh there's no concern about putting a guy out there when they're ready. I think so much of this game is earning a role. If a rookie earns a role and week one he's ready to go, he'll be out there. Uh I I don't think you have the luxury of red shirting players, so to speak. Uh so we we'll take it on a case by case basis, but I've had a lot of experience with young players that when they're ready, they play. >> So So along those lines, Avon could be a starter. >> Yeah, I'd say everybody, including Avon, has the opportunity to earn a starting role. I I think there's uh so many roles that are played in this uh in this game and it's our our job as coaches to give our guys a chance to go earn those roles. >> We saw uh Branch's role at Georgia and what he can do obviously was very good and that's why that's why that's why you got him. Uh but as you go through this offseason, do you try to know see what else he can do? See see see if you can expand that role. I >> I I think it's a good question. I think all all of our players I mean Zachariah's no different. Uh we want to see what they're capable of. uh we're going to throw some things at them and uh use them in different positions and whether that's special teams, offense, defense. Let's see where the versatility may lie on on our team. Uh so Zachariah is no different. Yeah, we're we're we're excited to because we know what he's capable of, but also there's you can push uh you can push and see what other things they're capable of doing and that can come over the course of time. It may not be just this weekend. >> For a guy like him and his size, you know, kind of get pigeon to that kind of slot receiver. What are the uh uh challenges for a guy like him to play more outside? I >> I think he he certainly has inside outside flex. Uh I think he's you know that word versatility comes to mind with somebody that can line up all over including the back field, including in motion, those type of things. So uh I I don't think there's a limit to where he can line up on the field. How long have players had like a playbook or how much of kind of the mental aspect for their preparation are you looking at over the course of this weekend? >> Well, you know, you're limited in terms of what you can get to them prior to this uh mini camp. So, uh spent a lot of time this morning ramping them up and and what we don't want to do is give them so much where they can't go play and play fast. And uh the goal here is to give them a digestible amount of scheme uh so that they don't have to think too much. Again, it's this is all new. They're figuring out where the weight room is. They're figuring out how to get out to the field. So, uh I I'm I'm um I'm empathetic of of that and understand that uh these are young players that want to put their best foot forward. It's not going to be perfect, but what we're not going to do from a coach's perspective is uh inundate them with all this information and then we don't get a true sense of of their their talent uh who the player is. >> Why should fans be excited about the guys um here this weekend? >> Yeah, I mean, they're going to get a chance to see them uh come the fall uh and certainly when they come out here and visit us at at training camp. I think you're going to see a bunch of young men that are are eager to work. Uh, I think just knowing our guys that we have already on this roster, you bring them into an environment where uh, work and and putting our head down and and and keeping the main thing, the main thing is what we do around here. And I think the guys that we're bringing in this weekend fit in that mold really well. >> You guys brought in a bunch of wide receivers. What have you seen from those guys? What are you looking for those guys? And >> I've seen a walk through so far. >> Uh, yeah. I I think it's it's a really it's an it's a good group. Uh just being out there and and being in meetings with with Coach Prince and and watching these players. I think that's the exciting part. Again, see what guys are capable of. Uh you have all this tape that you watch of the players, but and you may do some interviews, but now you get on the field and and you see how they retain knowledge. You see what they can handle. Then ultimately you you're full speed in individual drills. You're full speed in these sevens. And in competitive periods, you get to see what these guys are capable of. So, I'm wa watching these mini camps. It's fun live watching them for me and taking it all in. And then it's also fun going back and watching the tape because it's hard to watch every position on every any given play. But I'm I'm as eager as anybody to watch these guys compete. >> Jack Strand, another one. I mean, what do what do you what did you see from him on tape just from coming from division two and seeing that jump? >> Uh Jack was a guy that we did a lot of work on. uh watched a lot of tape on him, spent time with him as part of the process, brought him in for a visit. Uh very intelligent young man, great size for the position. Uh but it's it's a transition like it is for any player whether I don't care what division you're coming from, it's a transition. So he's got the right attitude. Excited to work with him. >> Good. Okay. Thank you guys. Have a good day.
