How much did you follow the Bears uh last year with kind of the the the last minute wins and the turnovers like high turnover rate that they had? >> Yeah. Um well, I just got just got really into the Bears since I got selected by him. Uh you know, I just watch NFL football uh whatever games are on, but now that I'm here, I really got to dive into the history of the Bears. >> What if Dennis Allen told you just about like your man coverage skills that he think's going to fit in the secondary? We haven't really talked about it too much. He just really told me I had good hips, good feet, and I was smart. >> What do you feel about your skills? I mean, they play a lot of press, man. It's it's that's what they need from their corners. How do you feel you'll be able to do with that in this defense? >> Oh, yes. I I I feel really comfortable uh being doing that. Uh knowing that I have good lateral quickness, good feet, uh being able to mirror receivers, and then just playing ball. You >> said they've emphasized competitiveness. How would you characterize yours? >> Like on a scale? >> However you want to. >> I'm competitive as hell. I'm I'm competitive. I'm sorry. I'm competitive. I'm ultra competitive. >> Okay. >> All set. >> It's rookie mini camp. What you thought it would be? >> Oh, yeah. Definitely. I knew it was going to be heavy install, especially, you know, with the Bears. I've known a couple people that have been through their rookie camp. So just talking to him is um you know just getting a heads up of what's going to be expected. But I think the biggest thing was just the amount of effort the coaches poured into everybody not just the drafted guys but also guys that are just here for tryyous. It's you know truly a blessing to have a coaching staff that puts in that much effort to all the guys >> were the guys you know who've been through here. >> Uh I've talked to um Dante Manning. He's from the Kansas City area. So just talking to him while I got here is good guy and of course he's participating as well. So you know he's a great leader out there for us young guys too. pretty full linebackers room right now with with veterans. What have they told you about what what your place is in this linebacker's room? >> Yeah, I mean I've talked to a few of them, most of them actually and you know just met him the other day my first day here and you know just insight I got from them was you know just be prepared be prepared to work every single day and you know coach Smith is one of the greats. He's been coaching for a long time so you know take in everything that he pours into me. >> What's this been experience been like? It's your head spinning like trying to take in all the information. Uh what's it been like that? >> Yeah, it's definitely a lot. Especially when you're talking about like the schematics of, you know, the defense that we run. It's definitely a lot, but I mean, you study it, you go home and or you go over to the hotel and look over it at night, you gain more confidence and which allows you just to play faster. So, just doing that every night. I'm, you know, not worried about it. I know I'll catch up pretty fast, but you know, it's definitely a lot, but that's, you know, what I love about the game, the process it takes to be good at it. Richard High Tower, the special teams coach had a big say in wanting you here and knowing what your potential could be. What has been relayed to you about what role and what roles you could fill on special teams? >> Yeah, I could be a core four guy and that's totally up to me. You know, I'm a linebacker. I, you know, played whatever tremendous amount of snaps in college football. Um, so coming over to NFL, I'm accept whatever role they put me in. And, you know, if it's core four, I'm going to be a core five core four guy to the best of my capability. So, whatever it is, wherever they want me, I'm going to be great at it. You played long snapper too, right? >> I snapped around for a few times back in the day, but you know, my special team uh like back in high school, I was a punter, so I wasn't long staffing. >> Not everybody from league loves special teams and embraces it, like you seemingly do. What appeals to you a lot about special teams? >> I mean, it's just a game of football. It's part of the game of football. You know, I love football. I love, like I said, I love everything that it takes to be great at it. And, you know, I'm blessed to have this opportunity to be in the NFL. So, I'm going to take advantage of every opportunity I get. And if that's being a core four guy, like I said, I'm going to be the best setter that I possibly can. >> How much more challenging is it? I mean, a lot of the linemen come in here, they have to learn the offense or the defense, but you're learning defense and you're learning special teams. >> Uh, it's a little challenging, but it's nothing I'm not used to. You know, it's something I did in, you know, college, even though I didn't play special teams too much in college. I was still in every single special teams meetings and doing the drills and all that. So, it's something I'm used to. Obviously, it's a little bit more complex now, but um, you know, I'll definitely pick up everything. What do you know about the Bears linebacker legacy with Singleary, with Erlacer? Just what information has been imparted to you so far? >> Uh, I know Erlacer for sure. I think everybody does. Um, you know, there's definitely been some great guys. There's some great players right now, too. And a lot of, you know, veterans that you can look up to. Um, but, you know, something that, you know, I need to do is, you know, educate myself on this franchise and everything that's within it. >> Your feet on the ground. >> I mean, it's been awesome. You know, this is your dream since you're a young kid. Uh, every single day is a blessing and I've just been fired up every single day for it. >> The Bears have expressed how fired up they were that you were still available. What do you sense that they were attracted to when you in your game when you've talked to them? >> I feel like, you know, I always have like I've always been a great team leader, been a captain for my team, and I feel like I always pride myself on my relentless effort. Like I'm always go no matter what. Like even if I'm tired, I'm going to be going like the fourth quarter is going to look like the first quarter. Uh they mentioned 60 plays. They they had a cut up of 60 plays that they brought to Dennis Halen. Did you have any idea of what maybe some of those plays were? Like what were some of your favorite plays that you think put you on the NFL mat? >> I I would definitely say my favorite plays are like chasing down screens and making plays where like I'm not expected to make plays like tackling quarterbacks like 30 yards downfield. Like I just really pride myself like I used to play linebacker in high school and I always was used to just running around the field and I still keep the same philosophy like if the like you never know if he's going to juke out five guys and then you'll be the ones who make the great play. So I try to treat every play like it's my play to make. >> Is that hustle something you you pride yourself in? >> Yes, definitely. You know that's something that my family's installed in me. Like I come from a really athletic background and my family's always like um like emphasized work ethic and everything. When did you realize your athleticism for your size was unique? >> Um, well, in high school I was a linebacker and I was pretty athletic, but then like I thought I was going to play linebacker in college and everything and then they told me when I went to Jo play and then play DTackle. So I feel like I'm really a linebacker and a DTackle body. >> So that's how much weight did you added maybe since linebacker day? >> So in high school I graduated at 220 and right now I'm 315. Yeah. >> As a player, what's your reaction when they tell you, you know, we want to move you back back in those days to to the Dline? >> Uh, when I was at Jo, I just wanted opportunity. I wanted an opportunity to prove myself. You know, I walked on at Jo and I just I was like, "Coach, I'll do if you want me to play punt for turn, quarterback, I'll do whatever." So, I was fired up just for an opportunity. >> It's still early, but coach give you one in particular. >> Yeah, definitely. You know, I'm always going to be attacking my technique. You know, especially at this level, it's a game of technique. Everyone is fast and strong, so it's always going to be technique. Were you dreaming the NFL the whole way or is that kind of something you didn't think about just trying to play as best as you can wherever you were? >> No, it's always I've always been dreaming of like when I was in Well, I was always dreaming in high school like coming from South Africa, I was dreaming like I'm going to be a rugby player, rugby player. Then I came I started playing football 10th grade and I was thinking I'm going to be a hockey player, hockey player. Then 10th grade year I was a wide receiver and then and then like as soon as I like got the itch I'm like I'm going to go full speed into this. Did the belief that when maybe did it cement your in your mind that like I can do this that I could be at least sitting here today? >> You know, I've always been firm in my faith and I believe that God always like if you really believe in him and honor him, he'll um really honor you and I felt like I've always believed in my faith and prayed God for for my ability and I feel like he's helped me and strengthened me all along the way. >> How do you experiment with jumping out of a pool? >> I don't know. It was just a trend back then. I was like, "Let me try." I mean, how long did it take to to get it? >> It was first try. >> Oh, really? >> How many times have you done it since then? >> Uh, I was doing it like when I was at Jo. I'm like, maybe I got to be a little smarter when I get older. >> It's a good party trick, though, right? Like, >> any other great feats of strength and athleticism that we don't know about? >> I don't know. I'm pretty open book. >> You ever like lift a school bus or anything? >> No, I wish. No. I mean, I used to help my dad like we'd work on cars and I'd have to like hold like the whole engine block while he's like wrenching it in under the car and everything. >> What do you think just playing all these different positions over your whole life? >> How does that make you a more complete football player? >> I'd say it's helped my vision tremendously. From when I used to play linebacker, I was able to like really see through the formation and see through like blocking schemes. I felt like that carried a lot to helping my vision and the D line and being able to still ID things because it happens a lot faster. But when I was at linebacker, it was like a prep for that. >> Couple more. What do you consider your signature moment in college? >> Um I would say you know just winning with my teammates like I've always prided like you know like I don't really look at the moments. I look at like if you have a moment you're only shared with yourself but if you have a moment with others you get shared with like a brotherhood forever. So I really cherish all the wins we had. You're an older rookie, but does any part of you feel like you're just maybe getting started? Like your your best football was just last year and just getting going? >> I definitely feel like my best football is yet to come. You know that we got a great coaching staff here and I fully believe in them and I'm I'm going to die fully into it. >> Thanks guys to get the hang of the offense and the terminology and everything here. >> Yeah, it's been awesome. I mean, obviously, you know, Coach Johnson is uh well renowned for his offensive scheme and you can see why in being here for the first couple days. So, um, couple late nights, you know, studying the install and stuff like that, but, um, definitely starting to get the hang of it and really excited. >> How many teams, uh, were interested in you and had an opening for you? >> Uh, there were a number of teams, but I felt like, you know, I felt like when it came to the coaching staff here, the trajectory of the franchise, um, and just the players that I had relationships with here, I felt like, you know, this was the best place for me to develop, um, and a phenomenal organization that I wanted to be a part of. What about the three players specifically that you'll if for the time you're here with Case and Caleb and Tyson? >> Yeah, I mean Caleb obviously, you know, I have a prior relationship with. Um we've worked together, have been good friends for a number of years now. Um had a ton of success together. Um so look forward to continuing that. Um Tyson obviously, you know, has done phenomenally for himself up to this point. Really look forward to working with him and learning from him just in the tape I've seen. you know, he's he's really elite in just how technical he is and how well he knows the system. And then Case, obviously, I think it's pretty unique because you have guys in like three different parts of their careers that have all been super successful in their own right. So, Case obviously, you know, has played at the highest level, gone to an NFC championship, um, played in a bunch of different systems and, you know, definitely someone that that I can learn from as well. >> You mentioned your relationship with Caleb. How influential was he and you coming here? And then on top of that, uh, I said that that wasn't the reason why they actually wanted you. How does that feel to know that you're here in your own right and not because of that kind? >> That never occurred to me, but I guess it feels good, too. Um, no, I mean, I I talked to Caleb kind of the day of. We hadn't really spoken like, you know, obviously, you know, he has his job and he's focused on a lot of stuff. I would never like conflate the friendship with with, you know, hey, can you advocate for me? I don't I don't feel like, you know, you should blur those lines, but at the end of the day, obviously, you know, he's a phenomenal player. We've been friends for a long time, and I look forward to working with him. What stands out for Caleb as a quarterback for you? >> Oh, I mean, a number of things. I think, you know, just his raw physical ability, you know, since we were, I don't know, 17 years old was, I mean, kind of second to none. I think that sticks out a lot when you see him play. Um, but I think, you know, the combination of of that and then obviously, you know, his his want to be great, I think just spending time around him, that's something that you really get to understand is like he really at the end of the day wants to be the greatest to play this game. And I think that that shows through the more you get to know him. Um, and then just his his ability to understand offense. I think, you know, the combination of those three is really unique and obviously why he's, you know, on the trajectory that he's on. >> Do you think people maybe sleep on I don't know how strong, how how fast he is. Maybe that gets lost a little bit. I >> mean, they definitely shouldn't, but um I mean, yeah, he's a he's a unique like if he wanted to play running back, he could. So, he's a he's a unique athlete. Um, and you know, I hope people sleep on it. >> Caleb said last season, like halfway through the season, he thought Ben Johnson didn't like him. Uh, what has the Ben Johnson experience been like for you two days in? >> It's been good. I mean, he's going to coach you hard, but I think, you know, that's why you're here. That's why you, you know, want to play at this level and compete. Um, and, you know, I I expected a little bit of hard coaching. Um, but I think, you know, that's part of what makes him so great and, uh, I look forward to to more hard coaching. >> What's one thing that you wanted this coaching staff to know about you from this? I know it's a little really short time, but >> there Yeah, I think you know that I'll do anything to to be around here. I'm extremely hard worker, extremely diligent. Um, and in any way that I can be here and add value, um, I'll do that. I don't care if it's taking out the trash or whatever it is. Like, I'm here to add value and help the team. and um whatever way I can do that um is what I'll be doing. >> What do you remember most about those years at USC with Caleb? Is there any stories? >> Yeah. Um I remember him like busting his ear open on the Heisman Trophy. Um yeah, I don't know. There there were a lot of a lot of good years. I mean obviously you know having won four games before um obviously everyone got there and then the turnaround we had in year one winning 11 games going to the Pack 12 championship and going to the Cotton Bowl like was a phenomenal turnaround um and you know the season he had winning Heisman Trophy that year obviously contributed to that. Um beating UCLA Notre Dame was huge for the program at that point in time. So yeah, I mean that Notre Dame game he had probably you know locked up the Heisman for him. um which is a really special moment for the for the program and the school. But yeah, I mean there's a ton that that stick out, but >> one of the toughest parts about the transition at your position from college to the pros is how quickly the windows close because of how much faster and better the knees are here. How do you work on that during this part of the year on acclimating to that and realizing how much less time you have to hit somebody? >> Yeah, definitely. I mean, I think it comes with repetition like anything else. Um, you know, there was there was kind of that that delta between high school and college. Um, and I think the biggest difference that I felt, you know, go making that transition previously was was the pocket. Just in high school, you know, you're kind of hanging out back there. And in college, the pocket was a lot different to navigate. So, I'm sure there are going to be things that that pop up that I'm like, okay, this is completely different. The speed is a lot faster. Um, but I think, you know, the biggest thing for me is just repetition and, you know, getting getting acclimated in that way. What was your contact like with the Bears before the draft? >> Um, >> uh, yeah. Am I allowed to talk about >> I just mean like did they talk to you? >> Yeah. Yeah. Okay. Yeah. Um, yeah. So, I I uh I actually I would say communication was not like I wasn't blown away by it throughout the early part of the process and I would say like two weeks before um it really ramped up and I felt like, you know, there was a decent shot that I would end up here. >> What? tell us the story of like when you got the call from from that. What was that like? >> Yeah, I mean so I don't even know like what I'm already >> um yeah I mean I felt like there was a decent chance based on the conversations that we had had previously that um that I would you know end up end up here given um that I would sign and not get picked late by someone else because obviously you get picked you get to choose >> right. Um but yeah, I mean just in my conversations with with JT leading up to to the draft and stuff like that, like I um felt really good about it and then obviously, you know, ended up agreeing to terms on on that Saturday. Um and you know, had some had some other things, but um at the end of the day, like regardless of the terms, the contract or whatever it is, like this was the best place for me and my development and the program and the franchise that I wanted to be in. >> Go ahead. when you talk about transport and kind of get an opportunity. Yeah. What did you learn about that process and how do you think that's going to help you here? >> Yeah, I mean I think my year at Louisville playing under coach Braum has helped me tremendously in terms of understanding scheme and system and my ability to learn it quickly. Um you know at at SC we were all signals at the line. We never huddled. Um, so, you know, having that year where I learned, you know, how to call 15 word play in a huddle, um, how to get guys lined up, motion shifts, more complicated stuff like that, like that has helped me tremendously in terms of, you know, the transition into the league. Now, >> that that part of it for for Caleb, he had to learn that in in the NFL, like how hard can you imagine how hard that must have been? >> I was actually thinking about that. I was like, Cam, like I should I I was definitely going to say something to him about it. But, um, yeah, I mean, he's I mean, he's well on his way now, so I'm not worried about him. But, uh, but yeah, I'm sure it was I'm sure it was, you know, even more difficult, and I think to do that and be a, you know, a day one starter in the NFL probably, you know, was all the more difficult. >> And then, and then for you, I'll my last one. And then for you, uh, when you got to step in and play, you know, you're sitting in all of a sudden thrown in. >> Yeah. Like, did you how you talking about college? >> Yeah. Like, and and you did incredibly well. How did how did you have the belief that you could do it, you know, sitting there like I I assume you're wondering at least a little bit. >> Yeah, I mean it was kind of a weird period in time because obviously, you know, we didn't go to the playoff. We hadn't had the season that we wanted. Um, but it kind of segueed into me getting my opportunity to be a starter in college. Um, so it was a unique opportunity. You know, I had a great support system. We had Cliff Kingsbury in the room that year. Um, and he was a phenomenal phenomenal coach and human being and mentor and someone that, you know, I'm still in contact with to this day. Um, so I give him a ton of credit. Um, and yeah, I mean, I think it was a it was a unique opportunity and obviously gave me gave me the opportunity to be the start of the following year. So things were kind of in limbo in terms of what direction the program was going to go into going was going to go to um at the position and that kind of solidified it going into the next year. So it's a good deal. >> Thanks, D. >> Awesome. Thanks, guys. It's going to make you

title: Press Taylor discusses rookie minicamp, elevation to offensive coordinator | Press Conference
text: I guess just to go back to owners meeting, it was the first time we had a chance to talk to Ben just about promoting Judo and he said you're like the most organized coach he's ever been around with like your library, your database. Like what what where does that come from? How do you explain your organization, your philosophy for how you draw help him doing that? >> Yeah, I think I think a lot of that started just being a QC for a while. Um, and I was fortunate enough to be in one place for a long time. I think that's a big part of it that helps. I was in Philly for eight years to start my career. And so, um, you see a lot of the same things as quality control. You're kind of you're breaking down everybody every single week. So, you see a lot of plays. You kind of, hey, I keep seeing this show up. Well, I wanted to just save all that. That's where it all started. And then as you go, it just adds on and you end up with years and years of the same plays or different examples of certain concepts. I was just always pretty good about keeping it all in the same spot, being organized. It gets a little bit more tedious as you build it out. Um, and then I was fortunate to bring that information with me on the places I I moved on to as my career moved. And so then that that's just a part of I've enjoyed doing that. I felt like that brought value to my role of whatever role I was if I could contribute video examples, ideas, things like that, being organized with it. And that was just something that appealed to me and was a strength of mine. I felt like >> Zach told us that uh he uses you sometimes as uh his personal encyclopedia for that stuff. Uh what was that like that dynamic you two? There's been some times um more in the offseason where you know we're discussing a play or something like that and I may shoot them a couple clips of certain things that have gone on. Um it's probably less now as as I've had more responsibility in certain roles and things like that. And it doesn't happen in season necessarily, but it's something in the offseason. You know, that's my brother, but it's he's also a football coach. We share the same interest. Football tends to come up when we're talking. So things like that uh come up quite a bit. >> Can you estimate how like how big your library of plays is? It's pretty big. I mean, it's I have to I have I know I have two different 10 terbte drives that I bring with me when I move and I give them to the video department and I don't think they love seeing me come down the hall, but you know, I I make sure they load those up for me and then I continue to add as the year goes and it it builds on pretty good. >> The most significant way your role changes moving over from passing game coordinator to OC, >> I think um just directing some of the meetings, you know, Ben's not able to be in all the offensive staff meetings, things like that. So, I try to just steer the ship in terms of where we're going, fill the gap when he's not in the room, relay his message um to the staff really more than anything and provide some some guidance on where we're going, what's ahead, you know, preparing for rookie camp, but also preparing for our veterans next coming in Monday again of what that week's going to look like when Ben's not around. Like, all that comes from Ben. I spend a lot of time with him or just he and I talking to make sure we're on the same page and then I carry his message through the offensive staff. How do you your process involves talking to Dennis Allen and the defensive coaches to get some perspective, some sense of what they're seeing in your side of the ball? >> Yeah, we're constantly doing that. Whether it may even be players of certain times and we'll do that throughout the course of the year talking to our scout team players of, okay, tell me what you saw here. What did this look like to you in your because we're trying to attack people in their shoes and there's certain times where we need you to play it this way because this is what we think they'll do. There are certain times where we'll say, "Hey, play it straight up and tell us what you see." And so, we're getting feedback from those guys. We are constantly in communication with our defensive staff as well. Al Harris, Richard Smith, any of those guys. What does this look like for your players, what challenges you? Um, and you're doing it just to get better as a as a unit. You know, certain things that maybe we can we can expose our defense to that we know people do as well, so they're seeing it throughout the spring, but things that we think could fit our arsenal throughout the course of the season. What do you think the the possibilities are for somebody like Xavian Thomas just getting to know him and watching him and obviously having scouted him? But when you think about that player, what are the possibilities? >> I think the first thing that leaps off the tape is the speed element that he brings. You know, obviously we know he's a dynamic returner. He's got a variety of experiences though when you look through his college career lining up at running back, taking handoffs from the back field. Um obviously being out on the edge, playing inside the numbers. you know, you see the speed and you see the complimentary aspect of what he could potentially be with with our group. He's going to have to go earn it and that comes in the meeting room first of earning some trust to get your reps of showing that you can be trusted when you get there and then being able to do something with it. So, just like anybody, he's going to put in a lot of time, put in a lot of work, and we'll see where he goes as this thing builds. >> Where would you say refinement needs to come the most as a receiver? >> Well, that's a good question. I mean, none of these guys are finished products. So, it's really just growing as an entire player. And so, with him, it's going to be different. You know, he he goes from Mississippi State to LSU, learns a new system, comes here, learns a new system that's probably a little little bit more in-depth than he's ever been a part of. And then you're doing it and it continues every single day. There's a new install. We're rolling pretty quick. So, they're kind of drinking from a fire hose early on. You want to see when it that point in training camp where it hits that they kind of they're confident and then you start to see their skill set really flourish where right now they're thinking. I mean every time they break the huddle they're thinking their mind's going a million miles an hour. We know you're not seeing the full skill set yet and that'll come as they get comfortable and they and they start to understand what's being asked of them. >> What did you guys see in Miller Moss in his tape that you thought could translate here? >> Well, even I mean rookie mini camp you just saw a poise you see an experience of a guy that played a lot of football. um the way he operates in the huddle, the way he operates in the meeting room was all stuff that we heard from the coaches that had worked with him in the past in college. Um and then, you know, obviously he has experience with Caleb, but that didn't really factor into what it was. It was his tape popped off. This is a this is a player that can play on time, that can be an accurate passer, that can win from the pocket, has enough ability to move around when need be. And then getting to know him just through this weekend, I mean, I think he's going to fit great into the room. And it's it's a really strong room, you know, with with Case and Tyson and Caleb already. We have experienced guys. They have a good dynamic. I think he's gonna fit in really well, which is important as well. >> It's a great opportunity for him, like for all the reasons you just mentioned, but why is that important for you guys to get something get get him developed? >> Well, I think anybody that's in our building, we're going to do our best to get the most out of. And I think a player like this that, you know, has potential to become a guy in this league or stick around in this league and potentially play, which is our mission is to find that out, put him in positions to see if he could succeed in this realm. But I don't think you're ever going to be disappointed to have a full quarterback room of a lot of guys that can play. That's a great problem to have and we'll we'll just see where we can get him. >> What roles do you think Sam Rous? >> Um to be determined. You know, that that's the fun part of, you know, we don't have a game for four months, so just seeing where it can go with us. Obviously, the year went where there was a lot of 11 personnel became 12 personnel became 13 personnel. For us, that was something that we felt like that's where our game was trending or our offense was trending as the season went. So, you know, you see a role from 13 personnel there with the way Durham played. Durham was a very experienced player that could do a lot of different things. We'll figure out what Sam's strengths are, how he complements those other tight ends, and then be able to use as many tight ends or as many different personnel groupings as we need to attack whatever defense we're seeing that week. >> With with Logan, what are some ways you guys will will test him over the next few weeks before the the break just to see how fast things are clicking for him? >> Yeah, I mean, the biggest thing is just the beauty of DA's defense. You know, he's going to see every front known to man and otaas alone and so then that's just going to prepare him. That gets your head spinning a little bit. you're making a bunch of different calls. A lot of things come up through the course of plays that were maybe discussed in passing, but you can't walk through every single look. But by getting all these different looks that our defense presents, I think that's really just going to train them and get them ready. And then you get to the speed of the game, you get to potentially joint practices, preseason games, all this experience just accumulates. And then we'll we'll see where these guys shake out at the end of it. >> What's the hardest thing hardest thing for a center transitioning from college to the NFL? >> That's a great question. Um, I mean, I think I think like any of these guys, especially interior lineman, every single week, there is somebody across from you that was probably some sort of college all-American or maybe he's a 12-year vet in the NFL. And so they and they all present their different challenges. Whether you're playing a 320 lb nose, you're playing a 300lb nose, it's super quick, or they're putting, you know, typically a defensive end inside in certain pass rush situations. That's probably not as much as you see in the college game. And then for us, our center really kind of drives the system. He's making all the IDs. The quarterback will reaffirm them a lot of time. He's making the calls. I mean, everybody's kind of waiting on the identification process from the center. I'm not sure if that happens in all the college systems. So to be able to be a part of that is really cool and I look forward to it and it's going to be a lot of fun. >> Probably uh most people don't associate speed with offensive lineman, but how does it apply to your game? >> Yeah, you know, I think the biggest thing, you know, especially in the wide zone, like we're running off the football, you got to get to your aiming point run uh and get displacement on these defensive linemen. uh you know these these guys are really good in the National Football League. So to be able to play fast, physical uh get to your aiming point and just run uh and you know the backs in this league are so good. So our backs will make us right. Whatever happens happens. But yeah, just being fast and physical. >> Have you studied some of these other outside zone offenses and you got an appreciation of what the Bears do run here? >> Yeah, I mean I studied the Bear I remember where I would watch the Bears too. uh just watching the way they did things, you know, the outside running off the football like then, you know, I come here and the fundamentals are the exact same. So, it's all just very similar in the way that it's taught and coach Rashard, coach Johnson, like it starts with them, but it was really cool to see and it kind of all fits. >> Learning about Coach Johnson and just his expectations of you guys. >> Yep. He's got high expectations. um but that produces results and you know we're all going to get better and when people expect high things of you that that kind of motivates you to achieve that and you know I I think that you know he's an amazing coach and I'm you know excited to be here. >> What are you trying to show most right now Sam? >> Uh yeah I'm just here to compete and you know that's especially as a young guy coming in you know your mouth it's going to be closed and your ears going to be open and you know I'm going to listen and absorb as much information as possible and you know every day I go out there I'm just going to you know compete to the best of my ability. Do you think your your uh major computer science kind of helps you uh absorb information better? And what made you kind of gravitate toward that? >> Yeah, I mean it's a real technical major. Um you know I I think that helps with uh just kind of general like information processing and you know understanding the situation and making decisions. Um I really wanted to do that. Uh I felt like I was going to Stanford kind of known for its computer science. So you know I figured I might as well do that. Obviously main focus was always football and you know we'll we'll be football for you know the foreseeable future as long as I can I can see but um yeah I just I wanted to challenge myself and you know I felt like I might as well take advantage of you know the ability to do that. >> Have you ever applied to footballing? >> I I did a couple class projects. Um, nothing super useful or insightful, but uh, no, I I think the, you know, analytic side of football is really cool and, you know, obviously coaches are using it across the league to help make decisions and, you know, you want to put your team in the best situation to win and, you know, that's that's how a lot of coaches are, you know, doing it. >> How do you go about setting goals for your rookie season as far as how much of how much of a factor you want to be here? How much playing time? Yeah, I mean I I I honestly haven't set any material goals on on playing time or um you know, catches or yards or anything like that. I just want to be on the field as much as I can. Um and obviously, you know, I'm going to do whatever the coach is asking me. Um and you know, again, I'm I'm just here to compete and you know, I'd like to get on the field and I'm willing to do that in you know, any way possible. >> When you first get your your playbook, I mean, like what's the first thing you're looking at? >> Formations, >> right? Why? So, I I've been told like when you're learning a new playbook, you want to start with formations and then you can go into kind of motions and shifts and learn all that. Um, with the formations, there comes the splits and then once you get to that point, I learn the runs first and then the passing concepts. Uh, and a lot of times with like the run plays or the pass concepts, the splits will change. So, you can learn those nuances after you've learned like the base rules. But, I think just kind of ground up approach is is how you should do it.

title: Ben Johnson on start of rookie minicamp | Press Conference
text: All right, here we go. Um, man, always exciting to get the rookies in the building. I know, um, we got a lot of a lot of energy. Coaching staff's excited to get going. Um, and really more than anything, you know, I know we'll hit the grass and we'll have walkthroughs and all that, but it's it's more about just introducing them to our way of life. And so, that's uh that's really the objective here over the next two days. Um, good start already last night. I I know a lot of information was digested and and we'll see it come to life here today. But um you know it's it's a great start for us this offseason program and getting them integrated with the vets on on Monday will be an awesome thing as well. So go ahead and open it up yesterday. What that decision? >> Uh Zay's a guy we've had here for for over a year and um you know it's just one of those things when we're looking at the roster where he's at where we're at um it it was time to to part ways. So, um, appreciate everything that he contributed while he was here and, uh, you know, it opens up a roster spot and and an opportunity to to make this team. >> Seemed like there was a lot of optimism about getting him on the field this year. What changed? >> Yeah, we we were hopeful and, uh, just wasn't going that direction. The trajectory was off and so, um, we decided to go a different direction. >> Scott, you know, who won a Super Bowl. Um, and I know he's here on a try out basis, but have you interacted with him at all last day? What do you know about him? >> I've talked to him a little bit. Um, he's got he's got a history with coach Randle L. Uh, Randle was with him when he was he was a young buck there in Tampa and uh and so there there is some some shared experiences. Looking forward to to seeing him run around and and compete a little bit. I uh from afar I've been able to see the speed, the quickness, and um certainly very intriguing. >> After after you get Malik Muhammad and all these other rookies integrated, they know what they're doing, that kind of thing. What do you want to see from a player like him that'll make you confident maybe in the summertime he he can be a challenger for some action? >> Yeah. Well, I think all these guys, and it's regardless of draft pick or undrafted rookie, um it really doesn't matter how they got here. We're all looking for competition and and we Ryan and I alluded to that a couple weeks ago after the draft. Um expectation for them is to once again learn our way of doing things, how we go about our business in the meeting room, walk through practice field, what that looks like, and as soon as they pick that up, then they'll really be able to compete for what is their their niche this year. How can they provide value for this football team? Is it special teams? Is it competing for playing time on offense or defense? um that's really up to them, but uh learning our way of life is first and foremost. Then >> have you uh talked much computer science with Sam Rous and how do you think that impacts his understanding of the game? >> Yeah, no, we haven't gone down that road, but uh but no, he's he is a very impressive young man. Um you know, obviously he go to a school like that and and take education seriously like he has, he's very bright. Um, I don't think he'll have any problem picking up the details with with which we like to play with. Um, and then a guy like Jimmy Dre who went to Stanford as well, that could be that could be a fun combination in that tight end room. So, um, looking forward to his future. >> You mentioned that the players the rookies learning your way of life. How different is the situation they walk into this year because the standard is set right away. >> Yeah, well, I mean, it's uh hard to compare it from last year to this year. We're trying to do the same thing. it it really doesn't change a whole lot for us. But for them, um, each college program is a little bit different. Some are run these days a little bit more like a professional program. And so the transition, I would imagine, will be a lot cleaner. Um, but not that's not everybody. And so, uh, we're looking to just establish what what that looks like for us on a daily basis, what what our expectations are, get to know the people, uh, not only in the locker room that they're interacting with every day, but just around the building that are here to provide resources for them to to be the best players that they can possibly be. >> And when you look back at draft and see 22 tight ends draft, just what does that kind of tell you about where where the lead? Yeah. Well, there there were a number of really good players coming out this year and uh you know, we were fortunate to get get one that we feel really highly about um that can contribute run game, uh pass pro, uh catching down the field. Uh we feel like we got one of the more complete tight ends that that this draft had to offer. But in regards to to big picture and just where the league is going, obviously teams have had success with the two tight end, three tight end sets. um things kind of always go full circle it seems like and it wasn't that long ago that three receiver sets were kind of the the norm and and now it seems to be transition on over a little bit more but I think the more you can you can uh look to attack the defense whether it's you want to give them in base defense or you feel comfortable competing against them when they're in their sub defenses it just the the flexibility that tight ends give you um I think it adds a dimension to your offense >> and from from all parties it sounded like Logan Jones's 30 visit here was a connection point for everybody. What for you was the significance of of that time together and and what it sold both sides on on the fifth? >> Yeah. Well, I mean, I I uh said it a couple weeks ago, you know, coach Roshar and Coach Dean, they they made some rounds this off seasonason, just making sure we we did due diligence on a number of players and and Logan was one that stood out. And uh you know, my visit with him um when he was here was extremely impressed by football knowledge, makeup, um very mature. And to me, it's it's not we're getting a rookie, we're getting a guy that's that's a little bit more of a seasoned player, which really is not uncommon for those Iowa Iowa linemen. So, I think he's going to fall kind of next in line for for a really good program, the next guy out. >> How quickly can he be ready to to play at this level? >> Uh time will tell. you know, it's the ball's in his court as far as I'm concerned and and uh he understands that just like with everyone else, we're looking to create competition and um consistency day after day and building trust uh not only with Caleb and the other quarterbacks uh but within that offensive line room and and then obviously with the coaching staff. So, um it's just a matter of time to build trust. with with Malikica, what what can learning under Al Harris do for him to get him to where you want to where you believe he can be? >> Yeah, I think I think for all of our defensive backs, it's a it's one of the better situations that you could ask for. Just I think the world of Al um we were very fortunate to get him back and uh he's a great teacher. Um I think he's very systematic about the process with which uh we want to go about our business. Um and and so because of that, I I think he's got some really good building blocks for young players if they trust him and they buy into his way of coaching that that they're going to have success. His track record says that. And so, um you know, I I think Malik is a very sharp young man and and he's going to be able to embrace that coaching style with with open arms. >> What are your comfort level not having an experienced long snapper on the roster? I know you don't play till September, but is that the kind of thing that could keep coaches up at night? >> Yeah, I there there is certainly uh an element of um that is is a phase that you overlook a lot of times and I think it's a good point that you make is uh we need to feel really comfortable about that position because a mistake on special teams usually wins or loses ball games for you. And so, um, that's that's, uh, an area that coach High Totower, Coach Bleven, myself, Ryan, we we've all been, uh, in constant dialogue with how we want to attack it here this off season. And, uh, we feel good about the two guys we have in the building. And it's up to one of them to to grab a job that's up for grabs right now. And if we can't get that done the the way we need it done, then of course there's other options out there. >> Ben, what drew you guys to Kaden Barnett? >> Say it again. what drew you guys to Kaden Barnett in the college free agency. >> Yeah. Well, I think he he plays the game the way we want to to play it. So, there's a physical demeanor about him. Um that's what stands out first and foremost. And um you know, I think we got a couple really good offensive line coaches that when when you have a guy that has traits like that that are harder to coach that you can you can help clean up the technique and things of that nature. So when when the mind's right, I I have a lot of confidence in our coaching staff to get the rest of it. >> What's his best or I guess what's his natural position? Because I know he's played right tackle, right guard. Do you expect him more to be on the interior at least to start? >> Yeah, we'll probably line them up inside initially, but um with all these guys, the best way to make the roster if you're not going to be a starter is to showcase versatility. And so whether that's showing that he can snap the ball or he can bounce outside, the more more versatility that we have in our backup offensive linement, the better off we are. >> A couple more please. >> Beyond beyond Roman and Luther, do you like when you have the wide receiver grouped or you curious to see what you have with that position? >> Yeah, well I mean we've only been on the on the grass for a week now. Um routes on air and and I I've been really encouraged with what I've seen so far. Uh, you know, I think when you look at it, it's a group that really complements each other. We've got a good mix of long speed, uh, quickness, guys that might be better suited inside, inside the numbers, uh, a few guys that are going to be able to thrive outside of the numbers. Um, so I like the mix and the makeup. Um, we're always looking to add competition and, you know, my experience has been you can't have enough of those guys. um particularly over the course of training camp, you know, guys are going to get dinged up and so you need to have a a stable of those guys to to be able to ensure you get enough reps for the quarterbacks and and everyone else. So, um I I think depth is going to be one of the things we're on the lookout for here over the course of the spring in training camp, but I do feel good about how that room really complements each other right now. >> What attracted you to Coleman Bennett and some of the things that he might be able to do? >> Yeah. No, I think uh Coach Dudesville did a great job identifying a player that he he's a darn good football player and instinctive. Um he has a knack about him that uh he he just is we like to use this term trim the fat and and you can kind of see that when he runs the football. He stays tight to his blockers and uh when you do that it's it's more glancing blows. So, it's a skill that translates to this level and and uh and so we're really hopeful that he'll we'll be able to see that here this weekend and over the course of the spring. >> Along those lines, did did anyone's conditioning stand out to you uh so far coming back this year? Anybody looking different? >> Uh shoot. From our vets, >> um I can't say off the top of my head. Uh you know, some of these young guys that that going into the second year, you know, Coloulston's made a big jump, Luther's made a big jump, as you would expect. uh and and those guys were around for most of the offseason as well. You know, you could you could go by the weight room and see them in there getting some work in in in uh February, March, and April. So, uh I think that has something to do with that. But, um no, I I think we our group for one week in in terms of the fieldwork, uh I'm really pleased with what it looks like. These guys are dialed in. They're very focused. Um, and like we talked about a couple weeks ago, the whole coaching staff is going back to the basics and and those guys are really embracing that mindset. >> Last safety is one of those positions where if you're wrong, everybody in the stadium sees it. What do you appreciate about his consistency that you've seen on tape and how that could translate uh to this level? >> Yeah, well, he's he's very versatile, so he can play down, he can play the post. Um, Oregon played him as more the Tampa Middle Reed player quite a bit, which which was showcased his his playmaking ability. He has a nose for the football. Um, but to your point, I think the thing that you see is when the ball's in the air, he's got fantastic acceleration uh to get to that catch point. Um, and then when he when he gets there, he he arrives with some violent intentions. And so that to me is what what stands out the most about him. Then the Iowa kind of an interesting casable mention obviously was loved there. What's it out for you guys to bring him in? >> Yeah, he he was one of the guys we identified well before the draft that um he's a player that we really liked and you know a quick quick story about him. you know, we we guys do a great job trying to recruit some of these guys we think might fall through the cracks and go undrafted and um you know, I I actually called him before the draft and let him know that we had a vision for him. And when you take a tight end in the third round, you're kind of like, "Oh, shoot. Well, that might uh that might take us away from from Hayden coming here." And yet, he didn't bat an eye. This is where he wanted to be. And to me, that speaks volumes about how he's wired. And it has something to do with with how he came, you know, walk on at Iowa and earning playing time and going through with it the long hard road. Um, I really appreciate that and I think I think we got a good one there. >> Awesome. Yeah. >> Cuz I wanted to see you guys.

title: HC Sean Payton on TE Caleb Lohner standing out at rookie minicamp: ‘He looks entirely different’
text: So, second day with these guys. Um, >> good second practice. We were ahead of schedule. Um, it's hard to compare relative to rookie mini camps prior, but I I would say um a real positive feeling just based on the numbers, the amount of guys um you know, seven draft picks, 13 free agents, number of guys trying out. Um, before we get into that, let let me do this cuz I think this will help everyone. Um, let me go through clearly with Bo Nicks where he's at. Um, he's doing great. He'll be well ahead of time for training camp. I think there's a good chance we see him in this offseason program in June. We're going to be the ones kind of holding him back, if you will. Um, the follow-up procedure was not a surprise. I was just talking to Bo. We had five other players that staged surgeries where there's a step, they evaluate, and then a second step. We had five, he was the six that that actually went through that. Um, no surprises. We feel real good about where he's at. Um, and you guys will have a chance to see it, you know, here in a few weeks. But clearly, uh, full speed by training camp. We just we just want to be smart relative to, um, holding him back a little. So >> any questions? >> Sean, you said, you know, it's not a surprise, but also the sort of messaging was that he would be there for, you know, for a full go and all that. So >> yeah. So look, when when let's discuss the process of staging. Sometimes after the initial surgery, there doesn't require a second one. I mentioned that we had five other players that had A and B. Um, I think back in February the anticipation was because we're starting in June, I think I'm probably going to be a week and a half, maybe two weeks off. Um, and I and I think you guys will get a chance to see it. Now, if we're up to him, it'd be earlier, but um, we're going to be smart. >> I'm not going to get into Yeah. No, because here's the deal. None of you guys know specifically what that means and and I probably don't know either. All right. Um, >> how about these guys, >> coach? George, besides the extension. Yeah. Over the course of your career, what's the value in that continuity and the relationship between the coach and the GM? Well, I said this to him the other day and and look um >> in our league, man. It's it's it's almost half the battle, you know. And I I said to him, I said, "Man, I consider myself very fortunate to have been with one general manager in New Orleans who I would call a very close friend and a and a great working partner. And then to find um another person like George, and I I know that we both feel the same way. We love the grind together. Um he's a tremendous asset and ally, and he's very good at what he does." and I think we compliment each other, but um >> yeah, I I'm I'm super excited for him. And I said that to you guys at the combine, you know, uh it was just a matter of time and um and and like we think alike in a lot of cases. >> Do you have any examples of um what a player or two did well out here in the past couple days? >> Um Great question. It's here's the hard part. Um the hard part is what what you can and can't do. And the challenge if you're one of these 30 try out players, you have three days and how do you make an impression? It's it's a really tough it's a tough um challenge. And yet we're going to meet at three today. Um our numbers relative to guys making rosters as free agents, as tryyouts, um is really really strong. And the first thing that came up in our team meeting, it's one of the first messages was, you know, the moment you're here, how you got here was the step the science of procuring the best room possible, but once you're here, um, you know, how you got here is really not important. So, um, overall, I I look, both QBs have done a good job. like when you get a bunch of this offense, you know, and and they've been in different systems, one's obviously older, the other one's young, but they they've both done a really good job. That's the first challenge. And I can remember being that guy and not doing well, like didn't know the fronts, didn't, you know, and and there's nothing that can slow a practice down more than a quarterback that can't get in and out of the huddle. and those two have done a great job. Um, yeah, I I would say the offensive line just in general when you when you come out and you look at them, um, you know, we were able to draft a player and then sign a number of guys that we had draftable grades on and it's an impressive looking group. >> Go ahead. >> What was the rationale of with Peterman? What what appeals to you? We always, it's always helpful if you can get a veteran who because you don't know how it's going to be for the rookie right now. He's been fantastic like spitting it out. He was just in Kansas City last week and you know, he obviously comes from football family. Um, but when you get a veteran, if you're able to, it um it ensures that there's going to be uh a steady flow to practice because you don't know if you're going to have freaking Shawn Payeyton over here that can't break the huddle and figure out what formation's which and dead serious. It can slow down your whole practice if you can't get the quarterback center exchange, if you can't call the play in the huddle. And and so, um, he's someone that's had a ton of experience at that. What are your earliest practice in years that you didn't call plays? >> No. Um, >> usually at this camp I'm I'm probably not calling the plays and even in the preseason, but like 2011 there's been a number of gaps in seasons, you know, where Pete had it or Joe had it. Um, but I would say it's probably the first for Davis in a rookie camp. and you know they you're previewing the script so it's scripting the plays and those guys have been good offensively you know there's some tweaks with the language some things that we're adding like we do every year um >> but relative to in season I can I think there was really two instances a stretch in 11 when I fractured my leg >> and then um oh there was another stretch or two with Pete or Joe. Probably Pete. >> How are you? >> What are your early kind of CEO role just through these, you know, first two practices, you know, >> I would say my role, if you were watching, isn't any different than >> what it was at this camp last year. I mean, I think Joe was giving the QB the plays off a script. Um, certainly you're paying attention maybe a little bit more to the offense. I like to look at the draft picks and then, you know, anytime something catches your attention, you're looking at the roster to see, you know, who it was. Um, this is I I think this is my 19th rookie mini camp and and part of the messaging at the start of it was I just can remember tryyous making teams here. So, your worst fear is that someone leaves here and then you hear about them later somewhere else. So, um they're all going to get evaluated. We're, like I said, we're going to meet at three. Um discuss yesterday and today scouts, coaches, get an update, anybody that stood out. Um and then, uh we have another walk through and then the final practice tomorrow. >> I'm sorry. What are your early impressions on Jonah Coleman? Is there anything additional you've learned about in here? >> No, good. Here is the one challenge with this camp. It's the only camp that we have in a year where there's not a pelon conditioning wise. There's there's guys that are in great shape. There's guys in the middle of the pack and there's guys that are in awful shape. And normally when you go into any camp, you've got a group that's been conditioning. Like when we get into OTAAS's or mini camp in June, there's a a BA level of conditioning. There's a Pelaton, a group, and in this camp, it's always difficult. So, you know, guy like Jonah's is, you know, his schedule probably was a lot different than some of these other guys. He's in good shape. Um there's certain things you want to when you're in this type of drill setting, you want to give them and then um he's picked it up well. Uh he's looked really good. >> So much of this is good for the young guys, but also you have a handful of new coaches on staff. How's that process? >> It's really good. >> It's really good. You know, we're coaching the coaches and you're exactly right. There's I don't know comparing it to the last three years, but there are a lot of new faces and new positions and you know working your way through the communication is something um that that they're working on, we're working on as as you get ready for ultimately training camp. But that's a good point. >> What are ways that uh the players can stand out off the field or or is it really just everything to do on the field? Well, today's we got today we got the most boring interview contest, right, with you guys. So then >> Drew, >> we we Yeah, Drew Sanders. The problem with Drew's was he was already nervous about just talking and then when I tried to guide him with parameters, it really messed with him a little bit. So we played the winners this morning. Um, Jalil 23, I think it was Drew, and then Bo, you know, who has the, um, so you guys can, you know, fire some tricky questions. Who has the most uninspiring, boring interview? Um, yeah. >> So, they saw runners in the uh, >> that's a great question. I I think we knew Drew would be a strong candidate because he, you know, um I'm I'm anxious to see, you know, we'll do we'll do the evaluations tonight and in the morning we'll have a top three. >> Sean, you always talk about how hard it is to kind of judge guys on just such a short time, but guys that maybe you thought were smart players, can you tell who's a quick study and who's just picking it up? >> You can, and it's one of the, you know, there's four things, five things we said. This is how you're being evaluated. You know, a does a player know what to do? Um, B, is the player trying to do what's being coached? C, you know, how well are they doing it? And then effort and talent. You know, obviously you have to be talented, but that's I think a a big challenge for this whole group because they're be, you know, they're behind always every year. Um, the group that's already here. Now, we've got a few players from our team that are out here and and um and it's, you know, it's good having those guys, but um I do think you get an early impression of the mental. >> You mentioned the the coaching staff a little bit earlier, Willie Sneed. Um can you just kind of talk about having >> Yeah, so we have three new offensive quality control coaches. Um I had the good fortune of being able to coach Willie early in his career. I give him a hard time. I think he played 12 or 13 years and I always tell him he played 11 too many, you know. Um, but he always knew who he was and he was a tremendous blocker, smart, tough, and he had to step on all the bases, you know. He was undrafted. Um, man, I think we got him off of someone's practice squad. I can't even remember how he arrived but he played you lose track of the years um you know and then you followed him with San Francisco and um when I reached out to him he was in Florida his father was a coach and and he was getting into coaching so he was excited about the opportunity and and the other young quality control coaches also they all have a good story and um you know you're look looking to develop talented guys and uh you know he just he was so smart as a player. Um and and honestly that had a lot to do with how he ended up playing so long. >> One of those guys mentioned you mentioned veterans being out here. How do you decide which bets come out here and what do you look for? >> Well, it's they they got to have it's really a a league rule based on pension credits. And so every year I'll get the list. You know, here are the five eligible. Um we may have all five of them invited. Um you know, I think we have three or four. Um I'll tell you who stood out, Caleb. Like he looks entirely different in this camp now. He was here in this camp a year ago as a draft pick, but he stood out. >> What is he doing better where >> everything from last year? >> Everything. And in fairness to him, remember, you know, that was a basketball prospect that had limited snaps of a year. And so, one year into the program and how he's moving, what he's doing, everything looks entirely different. And so, you know, that learning curve and growth curve was greater for someone who had far less experience maybe than others, if that makes sense. Like he it it's entirely noticeable. And he's in great shape. You see his athleticism. And I would say the one thing that you don't know is, you know, when Bill used to say, you know, if they don't bite when they're puppies, they're probably never going to bite. But there's a physical aspect to the way he plays and you know even on look team last season you know he play an outside linebacker rushing our tackles. I mean he's 67 265 lbs like and he's not afraid of the contact. So it's been good to see him you know in year two and and you knew there was going to be a developmental upside but that was encouraging. when you talk about the the learning curve with him, is it like, you know, you have these other guys who play tight end, you know, is it like, man, he's sped up now to where he's at their level or no, he's on an NFL. >> Well, I that's a great question. I I you just start with like total reps in the bank in football and there was just a lot less, right? And and you're drafting traits at that point in the draft and and we've done that before. And um you know sometimes you're drafting traits you see uh you know a receiving tight end. The one thing I know watching him is he's he'll be plenty and very physical and you know the blocking part is a little bit easier to develop than the the other part. But um you guys will see him this this June. text: Gordy, I have to confess I know nothing about kicking. Zilch, squat, nothing. But I do know when I look at video [music] of Trey Smack kicking, that ball explodes off his foot. It's kind of a prerequisite for to [music] be able to kick up here. But at the end of the day, what matters is getting it to the uprights and we think he's got great potential there as well. Another really good culture fit. I think he's going to be a a very good [music] kicker in the National Football League and again, it's the beginning of his journey, but he's got a long way to go, but we think he's got very good upside. You guys enjoy an excellent culture. How valuable is that when [music] you're introducing a new draft class into it? Yeah, it's important. I think I've always kind of felt that if if the majority of your players were wired a certain way, [music] that your your culture was going to be sustainable and that if you had some guys that maybe didn't fit, that it would be much easier for them to adapt to that culture. If it's the other way around where you don't have enough of those guys, it can be tough. So it really starts with the people you bring into that locker room and how they're wired, but I do think if we're all going to [snorts] pull one direction, if we're all going to face the same thing, there has to be a level of respect for one another in in that room and that starts with culture. One more thing for you, way back in the 2020 draft, you traded up in the first round and took a guy named Jordan Love. Now, has he developed into everything you were hoping he would be when you made that move to get him. Yeah, absolutely. I mean, quarterbacking in the National Football League is tough business. And uh certainly he had some things to go through early in his career to get to the other side of it, but uh not only as a player and the way that he plays on the field, but how he leads our football team, what he means to our team, his professionalism and and how he goes about his business. Couldn't ask for much more than that.

text: Pete, go ahead. >> Hi, Loey. I have two for you. text: Good. Good. How are you doing? How you been? I'm doing good. What did you you know, you and KCs first time you're on the field together, what do you think that tandem of you and him bring with you know, and what do you guys see on the outside? Yeah, you know, I think it's just going to bring a a problem. You know what I mean? I think it's going to bring a problem for the defenses, you know, you got two different types of guys to cover and not only that those two guys are both very explosive. What a I'm saying, did you lobby I'm sorry, did you lobby for that flag or was it called? Uh it was called immediately. I was trying to go score a touchdown. They threw the flag, spot foul, we got the ball on the 10. So, you know, it's a still good play, but I wanted the touchdown. How excited are you to work with Deshaun and Shedrick? Super excited. You know, especially like Deshaun Watson told me I've watched for the past years. you know, and then with Shedrick, you know, a young guy who is eager to just be better and and every day shows up with a great attitude. So, you know, I'm very excited to work with those two. Have you met with either of them yet? I have not met with them at all. You know, um yeah, 100% I can see how it could be an explosive offense. Especially like, you know, they I seen some explosive of explosiveness from them last year and then adding us two is going to definitely bring it to a new level. Okay, guys. Yep. Okay, thank you. Awesome. Thank you, guys.

Um, you know, it's also nice when you know, you have a tall receiver. title: Todd Monken, Spencer and Logan Fano, and KC Concepcion Press Conferences | May 8th, 2026
text: So, what were your thoughts? Just I mean, obviously you must feel like drinking out of a fire hose for a lot of those guys, but uh >> did you do you like how they took what you did in the morning into the afternoon practice? >> Oh, it was great. Um, you know, we've been able to zoom with the players that we had signed or drafted. So there was uh probably half the group that was a little more advanced than the second group. So some of the things we did this morning in a walk meetings and walk than coming out was a little bit easier for that first group. But first and foremost, I thought the effort was outstanding. And we stayed off the ground for the most part, which is half the battle. Took the helmets off a couple of times just to slow them down a little bit, but I mean it was great. It's great to get out here with the guys. >> What were your first impressions of Green out there? >> Well, I uh again, I think he's carried over the Zoom meetings to this morning's meetings and then walk. He operated the offense pretty well. I mean, for someone who hadn't been a part of it, eyes weren't always in the right spot, but you could see a couple of times uh some of the things he can do with his feet when plays break down. So, that's that's exciting to see. Can you imagine having special packages for him during this season? Probably too early to tell that, but I could say that anybody with that kind of athleticism, I think should he progress in certain areas of his game, I think there's there would be a possibility of him uh whether it's short yardage, you know, once you get in the low red zone, maybe some third down stuff that we could utilize. >> With 25 invitees, how hard is it to put together girls like Well, in order for us to function, we have to invite some guys in just to make sure we can practice without wearing down the other guys. But, um, I think it's awesome for them for them to get in here and have an opportunity to showcase their ability. And they've certainly got to get up to speed, but it is difficult in team settings with invited guys because for those guys, you're not giving them iPads. We haven't zoomed with them. So really they come in a little bit blind. So it is difficult from that end of it. But ultimately we expect that. We just want to see them move around and see their skill set. >> Todd, I know we've talked about in these practices it's difficult to, you know, tell a lot about the line. But, you know, when you have as many rookies as you do, what's important for Spencer and Austin and all those guys? Well, first off, it's it's unique in the fact that we've got like our first group that goes out there is you're talking about three draft picks, okay? And then you're one of our signes or undrafted and then you have one of our veteran guys, Jack, that's out there. So, that allows you to function along with some of the older guys. We have a tight end at running back, but it's great to get them in there. Obviously, they have a history of success, so it's easy for them to get frustrated when things don't go well, but it's just the start day one. And I was uh extremely pleased with everybody that was out there, especially those guys. When you look at the development of Casey and what's your kind of guiding principles when it comes to you keep them at one position and just kind of develop that or kind of throwing everything at them. >> It's a great question. I think you're better off at at most putting them in two spots if you can if you can keep them in one spot. uh that helps their development, but I don't think you can get away with that. They're going to have to learn at least a couple of spots, but you want them to be able to play fast to function without having to think. And that that was that's been difficult wherever I've been when you've got a rookie. Happened a few years ago at the place I was before. And you've just got to be careful of putting too much on their plate. But I was awfully pleased with them today and how they functioned, got lined up. You can see their skill set. He certainly could today >> with Casey coming off the scope. I know he's out there. Did you have to monitor his reps at all? >> We did. We monitored him a little bit, but he was he was cleared. He was good to go and he looks great. We just want to make sure we get through basically this weekend and and the first week so when the other guys get back and we're able to go like we are today and see what we got. >> Is that why he was working on the side with Christian during some of the special team stuff? >> Some of that was because of that and others we just want to get during special teams. If you're not involved in special teams, everybody has a role, so they get with their coaches. >> How about Spencer so far? How's heating? I know it's super early, but just your first impressions. >> He was fine. I mean, everything was fine. Again, I'll have a better idea once once we watch the tape, but um you can certainly see his diligence. I mean, I didn't I didn't see anything that would have, you know, >> made me think any different of him as a player. >> With with Spencer, objectively as a coach, when you look out there, you get to see him lined up against his brother. How cool is it to have that that scenario out here at rookie man camp. Just two brothers playing on the same team for each other. >> Not as cool as it probably is for them. I mean, it's pretty cool, but I'm sure it's really cool for them. And they they've been doing that for a few years now. And then to be able to carry it over now. I mean, hell, they're back there John right now. So, I mean, it's pretty cool for them. >> Todd, you mentioned some of the guys that player to have a brother here that kind of process. >> You'll have to ask them. I mean, more times than not, you don't have a brother here, so you got to figure it out. So, I mean, it'd be really cool if you could. I got a couple brothers. Screw it. You know, bring them in. But, you know, it is what it is. I mean, I I think it's awesome for their parents, right? Like, I had a chance to hire my son. That's awesome for my wife, you know, for her to be here. and and and it was when I first started coaching, I coached at Grand Valley State where my brother brother was playing and it's always going to mean more to the to the parents. I'm sure it was cool when they were at Utah to be able to go to one place and and get to see them after games. I mean, that's really cool. >> Todd, you kind of talked about the try out guys, guys you brought in. One of them is Jaylen Raer who's, you know, former first round a guy like that, you know, how intriguing are you, you know, intrigued are you when you bring him in, you know, kind of looking for maybe that thing that you know kind of went lock that made him a first round pick in the first place. >> I mean certainly most of the try out guys you're bringing in are younger players but obviously we want to take a look at Jaylen. He does have a skill set and I thought he did a great job today. >> Todd, how do you you make one of the guys to play fast? How do you sort of balance especially rookie learning on the fly giving them a lot of see how it goes. >> That's That's hard. That's That's the sweet spot you're looking for. But early on in the next five weeks after this weekend, it's our job to throw a lot at them, see what they're capable of processing, and certainly we can do it in terms of our system, streamlining things that we do for them because we're going to have to get them on the field. So it'd be silly for us to to put them in positions where they can't ski showcase their skill set or where they can't function and make plays. So got to throw a lot at them and then once we come back for fall camp really drill down as to where we want them. >> Couple more. >> I know it's rookie mini camp, but got the news today that Jeremiah was starting on the the list. What what's your mentality for that losing him for the season and the support that you guys have for him as he continues his recovery? I don't really get into medical. That's for somebody other than me. In terms of you involved with quarterbacks where you felt they were significantly able to elevate their passing I know when you were there with them but do you sort of pride yourself on a sort of a raw talent like >> well I was lucky enough to get Lamar a lot later in his career so let's not we did it we did some things with Lamar He was a already further along. But you can see that with Tay. You can see from when he was at Boise to then getting with Bobby Patrino and the guys at Arkansas, he's come a long way. I mean, you you can see that already. And there's still a next jump that he can make. It's exciting to have him out here and let him just play through some things. Obviously, this is the time for him to get reps.
