title: DeMeco Ryans Texans Rookie Minicamp Presser | Full Coach Q&A
text: What's up? Nice set up. Nice. >> [laughter] >> Now, good to have you guys out today. Fire away. Yeah, today we're excited to start our first day of rookie mini camp and for coaches, for the players, it's exciting for us as coaches to get the guys our first opportunity to get them on the grass. We had a lot of meetings last night and you're trying to see right who can take the meetings from the field, right? And you know, how quickly these guys learn and one thing I will say just from our meetings and what I ask of guys, our guys have been very attentive in meetings. You ask them questions, they're loud, they're giving feedback. Our coaches are doing a really great job throughout the meetings. We got some of our younger coaches are also handling some of the meetings, so rookie mini camp not only a a place where we're developing our our players, but also our coaches get a chance, you know, our assistant coaches, they get a chance to help out and coach some drills, also handle some meetings, so it's been a really great start to the weekend. Our culture here is set, so I don't have to say much on it, but I still have to make sure I teach our rookies what that looks like. A lot of guys coming from a lot of different places all over the country, a lot of different schools who do things a lot of different ways, so we just have to let them know how we do it here in Houston. May be a little different, but we believe in what we do here. We think it works. We build it around the people and that's what you notice about the draft class and the guys when you talk to them. Like it's built on really high character guys, Starting, you know, with with Rutledge. He's just a really great guy, loves football, right? He's He's ready to put on pads today, so I had to had to slow him down. But uh it's it's exciting to work with these guys, exciting to see them. And my main message for these guys is not about coming out and being perfect today. I just want to see how they progress the next day. What do you want to see them take away from these few days that they're here, classroom on the field? The main thing I want to see our rookies come away with is the sense of urgency that we have here. They're behind. Unfortunately, it's great you get drafted, you got a lot of parties, a lot of hoopla, but you're behind. Our vets have already begun working out, and you have to catch up. You got to play catch-up, and there's going to be a lot of catching up to do. So, I want them to feel that sense of urgency, and I want them to just also get understand and learn the guys that they're working with. So, you know, ask them to sit with someone different each day, communicate with some someone different, learn something about, you know, their teammates. The quicker we can earn that connection and get that connection and buy-in, I think it helps them along this process of a long rookie season. You got Sonny Jackson in a competitive punter situation. What are some things that you and Fred Ross saw in Jack that made you want to bring him in? Yeah, for Jack, man, we saw a guy who's been very consistent. He has a very strong leg, uh does a good job of booting the ball, had a really good first day today. Just you can hear the ball coming off of his foot. That's the thing that stood out about him today. So, having that healthy competition is only going to make make that position better, right? When it comes to the punter position. We got Kai, Kai's done it in the league, and now adding Jack is going to be really healthy competition come through training camp. Their enthusiasm, what you saw in their eyes before they hit the field. You talked about Keilan wanting to put on pads Yeah, for our rookies, you talk about the excitement. Our yesterday as walking through the halls, the first guy I saw was Febres. And just seeing him, big smile on his face, gave me big hug, strong guy, stronger than I thought. He almost knocked me down. But it was You feel that excitement. He's excited to be here. We're excited to have the guys here. The cool part about these rookie meetings, everybody in my meetings, everybody sitting on the front row to start the meetings. Everybody sitting on the front row, notebook out, eyes up, attentive. And I always remember that picture and I tell the guys, man, remember where you're sitting, remember how locked in you are. That's how you should always be throughout your entire career. That helps you to become a really good pro. So, I'm That's exciting to see these guys not only show up with that kind of enthusiasm, but understand that here in Houston, that's what our culture is built around enthusiasm. So, let's continue to have that enthusiasm through those hot days of training camp that are coming as well. On that one, with rookies, you know, I think obviously the biggest learning adjustment for them is more on the mental side. So, when it comes to you know, you're talking about learning and things of that nature, what do you think the biggest difference from them learning and being able to apply it and the people that try to learn it but fail to at times or struggle to apply it? What do you think is sometimes the biggest difference slash hold up in the application on the field? Yeah, the biggest difference when it comes to learning, it starts with us as coaches. As a coach, you know, I have to figure out how do my guys learn best? And that comes from spending time with the guys, doing trying different techniques in your meeting rooms. But most importantly, uh I think you learn by actually doing it. And that's for all of us. You get better by actually doing it. So, for us, you not only spend time in a meeting room, but we want to make sure our meetings are not too long, too extensive. We want our guys to be able to get up, move around, and actually walk through the the fundamentals, the techniques, the things that we're asking them to do. We want them to actually walk through it, and and that's how guys learn best. So, as much as we can put them through those situations at a slow pace, and then gradually speed it up, that's when you can see retention the retention rate really pick up. What do you think of K'Lavon with one of the top defenses in college football? How much do you feel like you watch him and say, "Hey, you know, this can really translate to our run stopping and what we want to do to clog up the middle?" Yeah, what I liked about K'Lavon from his tape at Ohio State was the physicality. It shows up, all right? When he's across the line from a offensive lineman, no matter who it was, he was knocking those guys back in the backfield. That translates to Houston Texans defense. We want to knock guys back. He does that. And he's still a very young player who has so much room to grow, so much room to ascend, but it starts right here today. You see him in his individual drills. He has the power. We can win with that type of power. What's it like for you when I'm assuming you obviously liked him throughout the process. Y'all make the first round selection, and then y'all go into day two, and y'all end up getting him. What what is that like? Is it do you do you attack the next day like we got to get this guy? Do you kind of regather and say, "This is our guy." What is that like when obviously you didn't select him with the first, but you ended up getting him the next day? Yeah, each day as we go throughout the draft process, me and myself, we we get together, and we we set our game plan for the day. And it helped by having a pick high in the second round where we can position ourselves in a spot where we see a player that we valued, that we had really high on our board, and he's still sitting there on day two. So, let's find a way to get the guy on our team. We we like K'Lavon. He we visited with him on a 30 visit. We really really liked the tape. We liked the visit. so man, if we added this guy to our team, we knew he would be an impact player for us. So, we found a way to to do that and that starts with Nick and his preparation and knowing, you know, the needs of other teams, knowing how the board is probably going to fall and him making the moves that we need to make to go get guys that we really want. What I What I liked about Marlon is you see a big guy, Marlon's of course everyone knows his story, right? Kids from Germany, right? Came here at 15 and he's been through a lot and he's overcome a lot, right? And to see this kid grow into the football player that he's become at the University of Michigan, strong at the edge of the line of scrimmage, does a good job blocking, sustaining blocks, running his feet and, you know, it didn't show up a ton, but when you see it, I feel like he can be a a dynamic player in the passing game. Big, tall target, good hands to catch the ball. So, we just want to continue to work with him to develop him. He's still a young player and our coaches done a great job already, right? Kaylee and James done a great job working with him today in his individual drills. What's your message to the guys as they leave from this weekend in terms of until they come back for the next thing? Yeah. As our guys leave for the weekend, the first and most important thing is make sure you contact your mother and make sure we understand his mother Mother's Day is coming up on Sunday, so make sure, you know, they show some love to their mom. That's the most important thing. But then, the football aspect of things, we want to make sure they're taking care of their bodies, they're recovering the right way, you know, they're they have to get back in with our veterans come Monday and they're expected to fall right in line and get into the drills with those guys. So, uh it's going to be a very quick process for them, a short weekend, but we're going to make sure we take care of them the proper way. And as coaches, we have to be conscious of how we're loading these guys from, you know, they haven't probably done as much football. So, we got to make sure we're conscious of their loading and make sure we get them prepared when it comes to our OTAs. You got a guy wearing number 59, plays the same position that you did. You got a guy wearing 59 like you did, plays the same position. What do you like about Aidan Fisher and where he came from? What I liked about Aidan Fisher, Indiana, you put on the tape and you instantly see a guy who is a great communicator. You see him pointing, you see him talking, directing traffic. It's something that you don't see a lot in college football, but you see a guy, he knows the safety rotation. You can see a guy who's very sharp. He understands the entire defense and how the puzzle fits together. So, really smart football player, All-American, made a ton of plays there in Indiana to lead them to a national championship. So, I'm excited to add another tough, smart, dependable football player to our team. All right. Good? Okay. Thank you, guys. >> Thank you.

I think you know a good offensive lineman knows what everybody's doing. So uh I think that's the way I kind of look at it. >> Was saying you can't wait to what was like just to kind of take some of these first steps uh of their first practice? >> Yeah, heck yeah. Just first and foremost a blessing to be out here, right? like you dreamed of your whole life to work to this point and um that's what you want to do and then yeah I mean you know as offensive lineman you want to put pads on right uh obviously you get out there and there's so much technique I got to learn so much I got to catch up on um and I'm going to continue to do that and we're learning that now but I mean it gets real when you put the pads on but these details now really matter. >> Have you had any of the other offensive linemen kind of try to show you the way or give you any advice any of the vets? >> I mean yeah they they've they've you know introduced yourself and stuff like that. Your early impressions? >> Yeah, he's all ball. All ball, all nonsense kind of guy uh just the way I like it. I mean, I want to I want him to coach me hard. I want him to hold me accountable and um I want to work together to go win some football games. >> What's the biggest thing you learned today? >> I mean, just so much, right? Like so much, you know, football's football, You got a zone scheme, you got a gap scheme, all that stuff's so similar, but just the way you're attacking techniques is way different. Um, and you know, certain coach wants it a certain way. So, that's probably the biggest adjustment to do it the Houston Texans way, how coach Pop wants it done. So, that's what I'm trying to do. >> Speaking of techniques, what are some of the things that that you feel like when you watch when you watch on film as far as NFL offensive lineman in general concerned, the difference between college pass blocking and pro pass blocking? >> Uh, I think just, you know, leverage. I think that's a lot of things like in college, you know, you can get your hands up high and you're probably bigger and stronger. Um, and you can get the job done. You know, in this league, you get your hands high, you're gonna put on your back, right? So, I think that's that's the biggest adjustment. Um, and you you know, that technique and those details, that's what makes a good players and good players. >> For a little bit, that did you know anything about him when you first met him? >> Uh, I mean, not really. Obviously, we went through the process together, saw him here, saw him there. Um, but as soon as he got drafted, just reached out to him and, you know, talked and since he's been here, I mean, he's a good dude. Um, wired the right way, really good ball player. So, I'm so excited to get there and just get to work with him. >> You watch? >> Uh, not really. I mean, they had crossover tape one or two games, just him playing at Oklahoma. Um, solid solid play. He played right guard. I played right guard. So, but not not too much. >> Your dream, but where does the humility that you have come from? >> Uh, I mean, I think it's just my upbringing. Um, just how I was raised. Um, just the faith I have like a lot a lot of things got to go right for you to be, you know, to put on them pads and play in the NFL, right? What drives you? >> Uh, I think you point to a lot of things. Um, I think first and foremost, faith. um it's rooted there so I can go out and just perform how I want to perform. Um how I was raised didn't grow up, you know, maybe the best situation. So I always football was a way out, right? Football was the outlet. Um just poured poured all my passion, all my blood, sweat, and tears into it. So I just love it. And you know, if you love the game, um anybody that really loves the game, they're going to be passionate and they're going to do anything for it. So I just love getting out there on the grass and playing. >> Very competitive. You're very competitive, man. We already talked about how you like to put your pants on already. What do you feel like it's going to be like going up against one of the the best defensive end of the league? >> Yeah, I mean it's iron sharp is iron, right? That's what you want. You're a competitor. You want to play against the best. Um you want to challenge yourself every day. So it's going to be great. It's football. >> Can you talk about the challenge of learning the playbook? >> Yeah, I mean it's a lot more than what you did in college, right? You're going to have I think at Georgia Tech, we did a good job of having a lot of concepts and a lot of schemes, but it's the NFL, right? You're going to prepare a certain play for a certain defense, a certain structure. You're going to have checks, you're going to have this, you're going to have that. But I mean, you just attack it anyway. You're a ball guy. You you take all the notes you can in meetings and when you're outside the building, you you soak it up. So that's just the way you attack it. >> What's your goal for your rookie year? And what do you hope to establish? What do you want people to be saying about you at the end of your rookie season? >> Yeah, I mean rookie rookie year is just come up first and soak soak it all in, soak all these vets in and then obviously go out there and compete. Um don't want to put no goals on myself. Just hey, I'm going to go out there and perform. Um get better every day, attack the grass same way every day with this head down, hardworking mindset, and you know them goals and aspirations, they'll come. You talked about little problem. What about the Miko that do you take away actually get a chance to be out on the field from him? Your your initial impressions of him? >> Yeah, I think he just has a joy for the game, a true love for the game. Um, I think, you know, you can tell it just feeds off of you. He loves ball. He loves being around it. He loves, you know, preparing young men. Um, and I just you can just feel that joy and that love for the game. >> What's the balance of you're kind of one of the leaders at Georgia Tech and you're coming into a veteran group. You don't want to get rid of the intangibles that you had there. You kind of want to, I want to say, feel it out. What's what's the challenges of that? >> Yeah. I mean, I think you just come in and show show what you're about. Um, same thing I had to do and, you know, I was been the same leader my whole life, but you go to college, right? You're not going to, you know, you're not the head guy right away, right? So, you just come in, you put your head down, you work, and the rest will follow. for you is that fun for you somebody who's gone from being a conference here say to the ACC with transitional period. Do you know that it's going to be something similar because of the next level of competition? >> I mean, yeah, but this is the NFL, so like it's it's a a step up from that, but it's football at the end of the day, right? He puts his pads on like just like I do. So, you just go out there, you compete, you work your tail off, and the rest will follow. Yes, sir. >> Thank you'all.

Do you plan on kind of keeping like a similar approach? Have you thought about that at all? >> I haven't put much thought to that. Um, we really need to see where everybody's at going into fall camp um in that position room. Specifically talking corners, uh, we need to see the growth and development that and Cam have had. You got DJ Dean, you got some younger guys. like we'll see where that room's at and then we'll cross that bridge when we get there. Um we're going to play the 11 guys that are helping us win at the moment. That could mean a corner on the field every snap. Um or if we got guys we like we'll rotate them as well. I haven't put a ton of thought into that. >> You don't have like a general philosophy in terms of >> No, I've been a part of rotating safeties every series and I've been a part of Kyle Hamilton's on the field every single snap. So, um, for me it's just you play to your personnel and you rotate accordingly. >> The the depth that you guys have built at safety, you know, getting Tony back, drafting Genesis, how excited are you about that competition? Obviously, you know, the expectation is that Derwin's going to continue to play closer line of scrimmage and figuring out who those two, you know, in the back end. >> Yeah, very excited. Uh, I think in every position room, you're trying to build a group of guys that are smart, good humans, great football players that all compete and the cream rises to the top. Uh, and I think in the safety room, we've created that. And so, you look at the youth with R.J. and Genesis and you got Tony, you got E, you got all these guys that are now going to compete. And I know who the guys that are have been here. I know who they are and I'm excited about them. And now you bring in this youth movement. Uh, and we'll find out what comes from it. Um, the beauty of it is you got Derwin, like you said, who's who excels at the second level. Um, you know, hopefully that unlocks our defense to where he can really roam around down there and make plays. >> Where are you at just installing the defense right now? I know not. Are you where you want to be ahead ahead of pickle? >> Yeah, we're we're right where we plan to be um at this point. So, we have I mean, if we're end of week one and phase two, you're looking at 30% of the defense or so is where we're at. And we're trying to build this thing conceptually put in the calls. Um, so it's a process. It's step by step. It's really planned out. Um, and I think we're exactly where we need to be right now. >> How big of a benefit does having leaders like you mentioned Cleo and Bwin and all that just as you continue to try to build build here? >> It's it's everything. It's everything. Um, I try to set the vision, try to lead the coaches of where we're going. Um, the it's the players defense, it's the players team. So, uh, having Khalil, having Derwin, having guys day on, having guys that are vocal, that are really good players that people respect on and off the field and that understand and believe in what we're doing, it's priceless. >> What did it mean to get uh, Dame Tucker in here as a undrafted free agent? >> Exciting. Um, like what I love about it because it's I like to think I'm a guy that carries a chip on his shoulder. Um, that's who Dame is and I think Dame's chip got even bigger for being undrafted. Um, but we've believed in him from the start. Um, I know who he is and who he can be. Um, so we're excited to get going with him. I think he's got a really really bright future. What are your expectations for the the back end of the edge room in that competition? Because obviously you put together a three with with Khil, Tulie, and Hakee. Got Bud as a vet in the mix. You've got Kyle during his second season. You've got Damon here now. What are your expectations for those three guys and maybe other guys that are competing? >> I think whatever plays out, we're going to have really good edges. Um that's kind of the starting point. Um Bud's been really good for us the last few years. Uh, I think at the end of the day, just like we talked about with the safeties, um, when we get into fall camp and we get to really now it's competition, we're going to find out who the best players are. And our message to the guys is we want the best players that make the Chargers better. Regardless of how long you've been playing, uh, what your situation has been before, we're going to put the best players on the field. So, we'll find out in fall camp. Just >> Kyle obviously fourth time pick last year and um organization was excited about him you know like a lot of rookies maybe doesn't go exactly how he wants it to go but we've seen with other guys in this defense the jump from year one to year two Justin boy is a good example have you seen any signs from Kyle that like a jump like that potentially becoming I know it's really early >> No absolutely um there's a maturity there uh he has been here from the start of phase one um he's bought in you can tell he's uh his attention to to detail is getting better. Um, all the things you look for for a guy to take a jump, he's showing them right now. Um, I haven't been around him much longer than these last few weeks, but from my point of view, um, he's doing everything it takes to take that step. >> You mentioned Don, how do you look at the back of the room there veteran young guy that >> competition, baby, competition, like coach Harbaugh says, competitors welcome. Like DP has been incredible. Um, I mean, I was one of the first guys banging the table to bring him back. Um, but at the end of the day, like, we got to assess where we're at each year. And so, when we go into fall camp, it's it's any man's game. Um, and it's going to be a great competition. Um, we know what certain guys can do, but we also want to see what what young guys and guys coming back that maybe didn't have as much of a chance, uh, Delshan Jr., guys like that are going to get good opportunities.

title: Assistant GM Brandon Brown on Giants Rookies | New York Giants
text: You guys didn't bring a lot of guys in for this rookie mini camp. Was there a reason why and why is >> Yeah, just the biggest thing when we brought these guys in for rookie mini camp was the instruction. You know, you're not getting a lot of competitive periods out here, it's who can take to the coaching, what's the attention to detail, and just focus on the core group of guys because we know we're going to be integrating them with the varsity coming up very soon. you you always have a pretty good uh background on how you >> you know scouted a guy anecdotes what what you came across in the fall Arll Reese what was the surprise level there and like uh I guess a good thing you had done your homework cuz most people told you it wasn't going to be there at five. >> Yeah. Well, with Arll it was preparing for every situation. You never know how the top five is going to shake out but with Arll was knowing, hey, how are we going to maximize them? Uh really talking to Harbs's vision. uh how Joe saw the fit and really Dinard Wilson talking about wanting to create chaos, be violent, be multiple. Um that's part of it with Arll, you know, that yeah, I know some people saw him as a edge rusher. You know, we see him as a standup will. Um you see in the past couple days his ability to command the huddle. That's part of the call it the attention to detail, the presence part of rookie mini camp. And then knowing what he can do like now you're looking at our second level. You got two guys that are 6'4 plus with him and Tmaine talking about depending the pass you got a rim protector would you say where it's hard where you're going to have to layer those throws and then also being multiple you know where we can affect the passer talk about blitz and coverage right you want to marry the rush with the coverage he can do it for multiple alignments you know you look at what we do with our with we did with Abdul in a vacuum last year Abdul can do it from multiple alignments so you talk about getting your NASCAR package out there deploying the rush um he gives us versatility allows us to create chaos and just create matchup that are in our favor from the defensive standpoint. >> Brandon, you guys, it's such a long curve when you start to evaluate college prospects. How much when coach Harbaugh comes in here, how much does that process change? How much does it change the type of player that you might be looking for? >> So, the process has been phenomenal with Hogs. And I say why it's phenomenal was just the clarity of the vision and the identity that he wants to build. When you talk about building the bully, all of our players from different positions, they have that mentality, a put pitbull mentality, as you will, where they may not all be in the trenches, but they bring something that's different. You know, whether you're talking about in the trenches from CC off the ball with Arll and then even Colton in the secondary, you know, Colton, if you looked at the beginning of the year, he wasn't a guy that was coming into this college season uh with a lot of hype. And he the big credit to him is what the work that our college department did with him. you know, starting with Jeremy Bright, uh Pat Hansum, you know, you're going into the season, uh that kickoff classic weekend, you were down in Atlanta, uh Dennis Hickey, and myself see him play against Syracuse, right? He's a guy that's not really on the map. Going into that game, our college scouts, Jeremy and Pat, they outline, hey, this guy's a double transfer. He's coming from Auburn, Colorado. He's got an excellent baseball background. He's a three-time all-state center fielder in the state of Georgia. This guy's got really good ball skills. He can run. be unaware for him. Game one, we see him game one, he becomes SEC defensive player of the week that week and now we get to come back into the office, tell Joe. Joe already had a feel for him. Now you get to Senior Bowl, uh Tim McDonald seen him live. Now you see him at Senior Bowl. Coach gets in, coach sees him, coach likes him, coach has experience with his, you know, his uncle Rod Hood and there's a familiarity there. We're not even getting into April meetings yet and we already know who this guy is. So I just think from the clarity of the vision that Harbs has painted and us executing the vision and kind of taking that call big ocean of players narrowing it down in that funnel to the guys who fit us not what plays for the league but what's going to be for us and lend to our identity. >> Brandon along those lines how has NIL kind of affected how you guys go about scouting and the guys that you're able to bring in? >> I think we've been able to get out of the get probably a get against really really ahead of the curve from the NIL perspective of just knowing the landscape. Why I say the landscape is the normal one school transfer now you're talking about multiple two or threeyear program guys. So if you even aen hood for example he was at three different institutions when they're at these each institutions they may not be there for more than a year or two years and their current staff may not know them that well. So, we've maximized our touch points, you know, whether it's onschool campus visits, multiple visits, all-star game exposure, you know, the 30 visits, but as well as a credit to our young guys, you know, we've hired some scouting assistants that come from the college landscape and they know how these guys work during the portal process. Uh, when they're actually have to negotiate portal deals, how are they with money before they get to us? We kind of have a beat on who they are, their love of football, what drives them, what are their motivators, and we're not waiting till, you know, their New York Giants know who they are. we know exactly how money is going to affect them. We know how they're going to show up every day. And with the NIL too, it affects, you know, really the quality of the draft. You know, you talking to our trade with uh coming up and getting Malachi. We're knowing what traditionally is in the fourth or fifth round. It's a little bit different cuz some of those guys are going back to school and wanting to maximize, you know, their value for the next year while also getting paid a good amount. So, we're just not adjusting our approach, but knowing that multiple touch points has been uh part of the success plan for us and understanding and knowing who the kid, what drives them, and how do we best support them once they're, you know, wearing Giants blue. >> You talked about double transfers. You mentioned Malachi. Give us a little insight into your journey with Malachi and, you know, how you guys came out came about really liking what you brought to the table. >> Yeah. Art with with Malachi, you knew when you went to go see him at Notre Dame, we call it our book of business, multi-year evaluation. You knew that he was a high school quarterback. You do a two, threeear study, you watch him at Virginia, he has steady production. You actually get to see him from multiple wide receiver alignments, whether he's in the big slot, a different route tree on the perimeter, uh what he can do in terms of the top of the route sinking for a big man, talking about working around the clock, you know, whether we talk about the playing above the rim. We see all we saw all that this year at Notre Dame. You go back into two years prior at um Virginia. You know, he's working I'd call it 6:00, 4:00, reaching down, adjusting his body for a guy who's, you know, 6'4 plus and really 215 to 220. And with Malachi, we knew the kind of person we were getting. He was the same guy at Virginia, the same worker at Notre Dame. There was consistency in the person, consistency of the approach, and then he shows up at senior ball and does it again. So just seeing high level of consistency in different arenas uh over multiple years, it gives you comfort of knowing what you're going to get year one that it's going to be low startup costs in terms of getting the player on the field and contributing force. >> Brandon, when there's a new regime that comes in, there's always the idea that after the draft, there's going to be big changes to the front office. We're two weeks after the draft and it seems like all your scouts and all you guys are still in place. What does that say about uh the process going forward? >> Unified operation. It's been really a great environment to be a part of. When I say unified operation, coach said something in one of his first meetings that has stuck with me and he called mission over men. And the mission for us is winning football games. Low ego, put your pride aside. From the coaching staff, having high level operators, great teachers to the personnel department respecting opinions. the ego being low, finding out what's best for us in terms of finding the right players that are going to help us on Sunday or whenever game day is. And it's a vision alignment. It's what is identity going to be, what we're going to do from year one to year two, how are we going to build it? And there's been multiple perspectives on it. And coach has been great in terms of the platform between all everyone involved, low and high, of if you feel some way, bring force evidence and show me where you see him doing it. and what did it lend to the identity that we want to be and there's been ultimate clarity with that and it's been a great collaborative environment and just not that just the alignment has been really strong you were in Philly obviously for a while before you came here and see an up close view of how they manage the cap I'm curious like two-part like how are they able to do it so aggressively and why have you guys not adopted some of the same practices they do >> yeah well every every club is different you know certain clubs tried to mimic other clubs um one I want to give my hats off to Dawn coming inside here and the really the balance of patience and aggressiveness that she's had. I think the biggest thing that she's allowed us to do is leverage our currency. And when I say leverage currency, it's your players, your picks, and your cash. And really doing that while preserving our ability to accumulate comp picks. And doing that is just being really forecasting from one to two years. And really part of um being able to use some of those mechanisms like option, you know, option bonuses and void years. Now, you got to stay healthy, you know, and we're on our way to doing that. You got to stay healthy and you got to be able to keep rewarding those guys that are playing at a high level and staying healthy over a long duration. >> I noticed you guys on the road, you guys don't pay attention to the senior and shrine. You guys are always in in waves at these smaller all-star games like grid iron showcase or hoola bowl, tropical bowl, something like that. Why is that so important? Because a lot of these guys end up out here for you guys. is again like Emmer's a touch point like the touch points are invaluable. You don't get them back and who's going to show up on a different stage. It's nice when you can perform in the comfort of your own stadium um your own conference when you're placed into a different arena and the pressure is coming high. Do you rise to it and do you, you know, meet a benchmark? And you mentioned that like hoola bowl was there like Jameson Travis was there and you see him at Auburn. Can he show up in, you know, against different competition, getting different coaching, and in a small window, you know, what does he do? Does he show up every day? Does he sulk after bad reps? Does he rise to the occasion and correct himself and string together good reps after having a poor play? You know, some of the flashes you saw at Auburn, do they become more consistent um when maybe he's learning a different technique? And just seeing him even um Skrki, you know, at the at at the Hoola Bowl, like Hoola Bowl, American Bowl, maybe, you know, not the the forefront bowls of of East West or Senior Bowl, but there's talent there. And we're negligent if we don't turn every stone. Maybe we find a player, maybe we don't. But we're not going to have uh any dialogue or see a player playing on Sunday or see him play somewhere else without having, you know, information on what can he do for us in the building, what can he do for us on the field, and how do we help him grow to be a part of, you know, what we are. And if he's not for us, we've already checked that box and know, hey, you know, we're getting our guys, but we're going through the whole inventory of players. >> Obviously, >> obviously with that kind of stuff, there's a big human touch, right? Joe's mentioned using AI as part of the process as well. I'm wondering where you've like where does that have a space in what you guys do in regards to the the scouting side of it. AI is a tool. Um it's no different than when you look at maybe whether it's AI, consensus mocks, um any other supplemental deals. They're all a part of the comparison part. whether you're using AI to synthesize information because that's that's the big part that people don't talk about. You know, if you're using AI to synthesize information of PE players that have certain traits, then now you're trying to extrapolate what makes them similar, what makes them different. Um, it's part of the process that you can streamline certain pieces. You know, you're not using it to base your evaluations. We're always going to trust our eyes. Our eyes, our exposures are always going to be paramount to any other supplemental tool. But hey, if there's something different, there's something that's an outlier, we're going to use that. No, no different than with Malachi. When Malachi ran, you know, 462 to 464, whatever watch you're on at the combine, you know, through, you know, AI, we having an E40, which our analytics department introduced in terms of extrapolating the game field. We knew that this is a guy that was almost 220 pounds that his game speed was in the 44 range, you know, and we could leverage that data to help us make predictive and encouraging decisions that may stray from what, you know, the the human numbers tells us, right? The human number told us 462 to 464. And we knew there was an opportunity point because if everyone had that data, everyone may may not have our other data points. And we leverage that and use that to our advantage. And there's multiple example of that where obviously we'll keep in-house that's part of our competitive advantage, but we use that to make educated decisions and really to really poke holes in our process. It's just all confirmation and figuring out, you know, what's the best tools for us to use at the end of the day and we fine-tune it throughout the process. >> Three more. >> Can't imagine there's a parade can't imagine there's a parade of scouts through Kutztown every year. Um, so you mentioned obviously the hoola bowl and how he shows up, but what was your journey in terms of finding Ryan? >> Yeah, with Ryan again, hats off again to our area scouts. Um, you look at Brennan Profit, our other area scouts that were at the Hoola Bowl, scouts that actually went into Cookstown and and did the work is understanding that you got a guy with his length, can he develop into being potential depth swing tackle, right? It's it's a right tackle that, you know, doesn't have, you know, live exposure on the left side. Ken, the tools from his foot quicks, you know, his set depth. Um, working his hands in unison in terms of the punch timing with our coaching and working with Bloom and Grant, can that be something that can be more, uh, call it consistent in terms of his set line and his punch timing and using his lengths just to ride the pocket and set the width of the pocket? So because just because he's a small school guy doesn't take, you know, him out of the fold. It's actually using those extra touch points like the Hula Bowl as a platform to see him against better competition. Again, for some guys it's to smooth out the inconsistencies in their tape. For other guys, it's seen him play against better competition and that's where Ryan fell. >> Bobby Jameson Travis is a guy that wasn't on a lot of radars. You talked about, you know, guys that fit you, guys that guys that were giants, per se. What was it about about him that that attracted you guys? >> So, with Bobby one, he's a guy that has gone the long way, the long way. Like, when I say really long, he's gone from junior college, um, he had his time at Auburn and he's a guy that came on the scene a little bit later, even though he's an older prospect, but you got to understand him as a person. I say more than anything, um, Bob is a great father and that that lends to who he is. He's a he's a young man with, you know, three kids under the age of age of five and a loving wife and that's what he performs for. That's what drives him. That's his fuel. And knowing that, you know, he comes from a large family in in Minneapolis. Um he's overcome adversity, but what you see in his game is strength and knockback. Like in the trenches, his hands don't always work in unison, but that's coaching. you know, when you look at DJ watching his tape, when you look at our area scouts, whether it's, you know, Scott Hamill, Marcus Cooper going down and saying, "Hey, this guy is a little bit off the radar, but you know, he has power in his hands and he can he can eat double teams and he doesn't get moved by side anchor and he can create knockback in a way that when we get into our meetings with Harves and Joe, we're like, okay, well, hey, we want to be thick in the middle. We want to be able to, you know, reestablish the line of scrimmage, create knockback at the nose. He's not a pass rusher, but what what he can do, he can eat two blocks and he can be firm and you saw the flashes. Then he goes to the hoola ball and he does it a little bit more consistently. Then we bring him on a 30 visit. We have another touch point with him and we understand the person and what drives him, what motivates him and can we keep untapping, you know, and sharpening his tools in terms of making him a consistent player um where we took him and really take getting to understand him is understand that yes, he's a guy that we drafted later, but we're just as excited about him as guys that went higher in the draft. We just knew the opportunity for us was later on because of maybe some of the perceived warts from, you know, universally, but for us, man, we're excited Bobby's here and we're excited to keep grooming him. >> With Arvel and Abdul, you mentioned both of them versatility. How much is that a priority now with just kind of looking for defensive guys who not only have just say a great skill set, but can do so many different things on the field? >> It's it's really evident. It's being multiple and it's understanding what's going to play in this scheme as a premium. You know, I previously worked with Dinard Wilson before and um the defense is really going to take on a lot of his personality. It's going to be aggressive. It's going to be multiple. You know, you're going to feel pressure from different alignments. And when you have guys that can fit different hats, you don't got to take him off the field. You know, we can go from base to sub and move guys around and you're going to have to identify where pressure is coming from and you may not know and you may see think that hey Arbell's is is a threat as a interior interior rusher and then he's lining up on the edge or you know he's he's dropping in in the hook area or you're looking at Burns or Abdul. They can all do the same thing. So, it's us finding the best matchup week to week, having multiple guys that can do multiple roles allows us to expose whatever that weak point will be in that weekly matchup. And it it fits Dinard's style. Um, it's a guy that we've loved from, you know, day one. You know, didn't think he'd be there when we took him. Uh, but to get to know him is he's a guy that you want next to you, you know, in the thick of the fight. You know, the one thing that stuck out for me that he said on the first interaction was when all else fail, speed and violence is my game. And I know with him, he's a sponge. He's a guy that's overcome a lot of adversity. It's going to be cool for you guys to understand and learn his story the more you get around him. Um, but he's a he's a survivor and he's a guy that um does it in the most humblest way. You know, he's embrace a new environment, but at the same time, um, he's ready for the new occasion. He's he's ready for the big stage. Anything that comes his way, you know, as he metriculates and gets back into the film with the varsity, um he's going to take it head on and uh he's going to be a sponge and excited to keep working with them.

title: Colton Hood Speaks to the media after Giants Rookie Minicamp | New York Giants
text: Take us through that play where you got the the interception there. Um yeah, we was just in cover two. My guy went in and went short, so you know, I had to run back to my flat and I just broke on the ball and made a play. How did it end up in your hands? I took it from him. Would you say that was more physical than it needed to be for a camp like this? Nah. I mean, I got to get paid, too, so. >> [laughter] >> You No no celebration until the coaches urged you to do it. >> Yeah, I mean, it's practice, so you know, I'm not really going to celebrate on my teammates, but you know what I'm saying? It's definitely going to come out when the season starts, for sure. Seems that picked up a lot of steam like you the coaches like they're all over it. They're asking you about it in the interviews and stuff. What What do you think of that? Yeah, I think it's pretty cool. I didn't really expect it to get this big, you know, I've seen other players from different teams use it with It really ain't the same cuz their name last name is not Hood, but you know, it's been It's been really cool just to see it pick up like that and you know, I'm going to keep doing it the rest of my career. Is there a name to that or No. Nah, it's just the Hood, I guess. What What are your early impressions of Coach Harbaugh today? Um shoot, great coach. I mean, he coaches hard. He wants his guys to be great. You know, he gives good feedback, too, when you do the do good and do the right thing, so you know, he's a great coach and you know, I'm I'm really enjoying being here, for sure. Did he say anything to you after the Um play you made? Nah, I didn't speak to him, but I probably will later. Which coach asked you to do the Uh it was Coach Addison Lynch. He's our corners coach. Kool-Aid, when you were at Tennessee, did you primarily play left cornerback or right cornerback or did you travel? Yeah, I was usually traveling to, you know, whoever the best guy was. That's That's what I usually did. But did you were mostly on the left side though or I played both sides. It just depended where it where they lined up. What are your early impressions of Malachi Fields? Um big, strong, physical, catches everything, you know. Um you know, you always need a guy like that, you know, on the other side of the ball. He can stretch the field. He's got good speed, too, sneaky speed. So, you know, I'm excited to continue to compete with him in practice and, you know, get better. Your uncle told you strong points for you with Ar'vion. You just played for him, but you didn't see him firsthand. Was it any different than what your uncle told you about what to expect from him? Nah, it wasn't. Um shoot, my uncle told me what to expect and it was everything, you know, I expected, so. And what was that? You said be like old school, hard nose. >> Yeah, just a hard nose. He's always old school, but he loves his players. He bigs them up. He wants them to be great, so you know, it's a it's that tough love kind of thing, for sure. Cole, there are always videos that come out from draft night. You know, we know your situation and what happened, but when Ar'vion got picked, he kind of had a couple guys like waiting to greet him and you were one of them. Now, I don't know if you were friendly beforehand, but it's kind of ironic the next day. I mean, do you remember that moment? Was that important for you to kind of engage with other guys or was Yeah, yeah. It definitely was, especially Ar'vion. We trained together in Tampa um for the combine. You know, we signed to the same agency. Um you know, that's He's one of my good friends, you know. I'm excited, you know, I want to see all my friends win, you know what I'm saying? So, when he got picked, you know, I was excited and then ended up that we both on the same team, so. One thing I noticed about your game is that you you're not shy when the ball comes your way. Just supposed most DBs, they panic and they lose sight of what's going on. Where did that come come from and why do most DBs panic? Um I think a lot of DBs panic just cuz, you know, they're not good at tracking the ball. I played baseball, played center field, so tracking a football is 10,000 times easier than tracking a baseball, so, you know, it's easy. I mean, I wouldn't say it's easy, but um it's something that, you know, I've been doing my whole life, so um it comes natural to me. Why will Ar'vion be a problem? Shoot. I mean, you see how big he is. Like, he came up there, he probably looked like the Hulk, you know what I'm saying? But, just just, you know, his physic his physical abilities and then not just that, but he's a smart football player. He knows football so, you know, that's why he going to be a problem for sure. Cole, you were pretty good against the run in Tennessee. I mean, what what does it take to play the run as a small you have to you're small but but you know >> Yeah, um tackling is a mentality, you know what I'm saying? Just just having that mentality to just want to go out there and you know, dominate in every facet of the game um definitely help me. So, it's really just my mentality. I know you've been in the defense for like 2 days now but what stands out of what they're going to ask corners to do? Um yeah, shoot they want us to you know, be up in guys' faces. That's what I like to do. You know, and just you know, being able to be cerebral. It's not very hard but you know, you can see how complex it is together so, you know, how it can you know, affect offenses and you know, have them to be tripping up, you know, what I'm saying when when the play comes so, I'm really excited to continue to learn and do what I need to do. When the veterans roll in here next week and you guys kind of get to mesh finally in the locker room, what is it about your personality or your approach that you think will make it an easy transition for you? Yeah, you know, I think I'm a I'm a kind of a kind of a harder person light-hearted, you know, what I'm saying? And you know, I'm not too serious but I'm about my business at the same time.
