He's got some familiarity with the Bucks, too. He's had some guys he's worked with that have been here. >> Uh, yeah, just stay grounded, you know, get in that playbook, you know. Um, you know, they going to see your potential. Just keep working hard. They threw a lot at you guys, but the quarterback Jaylen Daniels you were working with yesterday, what was your impression of him having to handle that the first day? >> Yeah. Yeah, I I know that probably is a lot on his and just having to know every route and everything and the protection and all of this. So, I commend to him for sure. He had a great day. >> Do you want us to refer to you as Hurst the third or just Hurst? >> Uh, Hurst. Hurst will be okay. >> Okay. >> What do you prefer? You said >> Yeah, hers will be Hurst will be okay. T, you're coming into this room with with an established guy in Chris God within, number two receiver in Bucks history, as well as some younger receivers that are more your age that have also had a lot of early success. What does that mean to come in and just have a a bank of people that have had success here with Baker Mabel throwing the ball that can help accelerate your learning curve? >> Yeah, definitely. I, you know, I'm going whenever they get around, you know, try to stick in those guys, you know, hit pocket and learn, you know, everything they learn. I I know they're probably going to be willing to teach me anyway, so definitely be in that help pocket. >> Wade mentioned that you graduated from Georgia State. Yeah. Congratulations on that. >> How important was that to you to make sure that you did that before beginning your NFL career? >> Yeah, I kind of was really ready to get here. I didn't want to miss anything, but you know, that's a big piece for my mom, you know, having five kids, four her kids graduated. So, you know, that was a big thing. Big deal. >> Anything else? >> Thanks. Thanks a lot. >> Thank you guys. Not bread.

title: Todd Bowles: Rueben Bain Jr. Looks in ‘Midseason Form’ | Press Conference | Tampa Bay Buccaneers
text: afternoon. I don't know how much you're able to watch or focus on any particular position out there, but just seeing Ruben come off the ball, how how quick he is and and you know, few of those he probably would have had sacks on, but just what was your impression of how he was today? >> He looked like he was in mid-season form. Obviously, he's from Miami, so he's going to be practicing in the heat where a lot of the other guys are going to struggle to adjust to this weather, so it didn't bother him at all. He came in in great shape, and he ran around well, and he kind of picked up some things very well. >> What do you look for in these, you've been doing this a long time, these first few days as the, you know, college guys get adjusted to, you know, facing up against some pro guys? What do you look for as they start adjusting to this pro game? >> The biggest thing is not the same make the same mistake two or three times in a row. You can make different ones as the install grows and you get yourselves in shape. You got to make sure when you make a mistake, you learn from it and come back from that. If you keep making the same mistakes over and over again, that kind of tells the story. But these guys have been studying, so we'll come back tomorrow and see what they learn from today and not make that same mistake and the install will grow and see how much they can comprehend from there. But that's the most part that what we're looking for. You guys have had so much success with with undrafted rookies, not only making the 53, but but playing and helping the team. Is there is there a player or position uh that you're excited that you saw today that that could could have a chance to that this year? >> Not that I've seen today. Um I'm sure we're going to have to wait for training camp and pads for something like that to show up, but we're just trying to see if these guys what kind of shape they're in as well. So, a lot of these guys been working out indoors or at different places that haven't had the same humidity and it's not overly hot down here for us, but for them it's kind of a little bit of a culture shock. So, we got to be careful with that as well. So, I think that'll reveal itself in training camp. >> Todd, when you're lining up on your center doing your your installs and playing quarterback, what are you looking for? Or is that a good vantage point for you to see how the rush comes or why why do you >> operate as a quarterback? >> I can see defensively who has a vein in their head and may need to see it again or if they do the wrong thing, I can put it in a formation to where they learn from it and correct mistakes better that way. I can see everybody's eyes and I can see everybody face and it's it's more for me not to play quarterback but for me to see the entire picture and know who needs it again and who may miss something. And when they coaches tell them something and they still got a vein in their head, they didn't comprehend it. So, I'll probably need to run that play again so they can get that. So, it it's a good view for me to see whether they're getting it or not. >> How often do you do that and when did you start doing that as a coach? >> Oo. I mean, I've done it forever. Obviously, ever since I've become a defensive coordinator, which is probably years ago now. So, I do it a lot. uh especially in the walkth through because that's when we're teaching the most and we're getting everything down and so it it's not for me because I'm far past my quarterback days. It's really for me to see the other side of the ball so we can get it right. >> Obviously Kante Scott has a cast right now. But what uh we saw Damonte Kapart out today. What is he dealing with? >> Uh he has a wrist as well. He can do some things but we want to get it fully healed up. when Kante is back and playing um obviously you know playing with Ruben but what is he is a nickel first and foremost and is his ability to be that chess piece that can blitz tackle what do you like about him in the nickel spot >> he's probably even with his size he plays more like a linebacker and Parish plays a great nickel and Paris was a cover guy and Paris is tough and he can tackle he he's one of the few guys that runs a 4-3 talking about Keonte that plays a 4-3 Y, you can really see it in his play, in his explosion. He's very instinctive and Paris was all rookie and it's still he's still going to play in there as well, but we're going to get him some more outside reps. We're going to start Kee out as nickel. Then we'll see if he involves to whether it becomes a safety or a corner from that standpoint and go from there. But, you know, he he's really a guy that can play all over the place. Allows us to play with 60B some and keep him and Parish inside. So, he gives us a lot of options. You're saying that Keonte could potentially, you know, also get some reps at outside corner, too. >> Yeah, we're gonna look at him. I mean, we got to move our guys around because when you make cuts, you don't have that many. So, we got to be able to have some versatile pieces. >> Look like Ted Hurst was moving around out there. He had a nice catch towards the end of the period at the end. What did you see from him and how would you evaluate his first game? >> Oh, great size, very good athlete. Obviously, he's got to get used to the heat a little bit himself. even though he's from Georgia, he's got to get used to the heat a little bit. But you can see the athleticism and the size and what you liked about him coming out from the draft. So, he's just going to get better and better as he learns the system and gets more comfortable, but he looks good on the hoof and he moves very smoothly. >> What does it do for you? You mentioned Bane's used to the heat and all that. What does it do for you when you have a player who will practice that hard? Like, you know, you want all your guys to do that, right? And most for the most part, they do, but he's not going to take a rep off. >> No, he's not. And it brings a certain attitude to your to your defense. Obviously, we tried to get a couple of those guys in there this year. Obviously, with Bane's uh Asan's attitude and just talking about the newcomers, Troder and Keonte as well along with Kanye and all the guys we already have on defense, you know, it just helps bring them closer together and makes them push each other to work harder. >> You've seen Marcus West Indie defensive line coach on the grass a little bit now. What are your thoughts on his coaching style and what he can bring to the defensive line room? >> Outstanding teacher. I think he sweats out there and works harder more than anybody out there. Love him as a teacher. I I told him I don't know CPR, so I can't give him mouth to mouth if he passes out, but he does a very good job explaining the game to those guys and he's he's been a great surprise. >> Todd, when it comes to linebacker, what do you like about Josiah Troder? Uh, and what do you want to see from him, not just in rookie mini camp, but as the offseason progresses? >> Well, adapting to the system, number one. We know he can go downhill. We know he's a very good blitzer. We know he's a very good shock and shed guy. We know he's a very good tackler. We know he understands zone concepts and he can play on the edge as an outside backer if need be and he can play inside. So, just the same things that he did in college, but it's about grasping the system and understanding what you can take advantage of. And, you know, he's got great pedigree and he's a very smart player himself. So, I just look for him to get better and better. >> Where is his ceiling potentially in terms of coverage? I know I had asked that of others um right after the draft, but didn't get a chance to ask you that. >> I mean, he's not Derek Brooks and Levante David. That's not his style. But he can cover. They never asked him to cover. I've seen him cover before. Uh I've seen him work out probably in high school just by default at being at a place at the right time. But, you know, he he's very capable cover guy. He's a good four sixish guy and he can hold his own and he understands angles and I'm not worried about it. >> What about the mental aspect of that too? Obviously, he's got a I'm sure a very high football IQ and and and it's in his blood and and he's been around the game for such a long time, but in terms of like how much his instincts could potentially help him master that aspect of the game, >> that'll help him more once he gets comfortable in the system. Obviously, the more we put in, the more he gets comfortable with, the more you'll see his instincts make a play. >> It's not often that you have a guy change sides of the ball at the NFL level, but you guys are doing that with with Nash Hutmaker, moving him from DTack to guard. just ask you what you like about that and what he has to do to kind of take on the other side of the ball. >> When we got him last year, we we talked about it. Me and Jason talked about it as soon as we got him in the beginning and we knew he was very tough and we knew he's very smart and he never got moved out of there by the offensive guys and with the depth we had at Dline and he's a little bit slower of foot that way, we thought he'd make a great guard because he's compact, he's very intelligent, he's extremely tough and he can figure things out and you're not going to run him over. So, it would be a good idea. We talked about it before last season. Obviously, with everybody hurt, we didn't get a chance to do it and try to help him out. So, this year, uh, I think he has a chance to make an impact at guard. So, we're going to see what he can do. >> One of those defensive linemen that you were talking about in terms of depth was Jason Jones, who I think was showing some promise in the practice squad before he got hurt on on IR. What do you like about Jason Jones's game? >> Heavy-handed. You know, he's the prototypical for technique. He's good 6'5, 66. He's 300 something pounds. He can two gap and take on blockers and shock and shed people. Uh working on his pass rush game, but in the run game, you know, he's a brick wall. >> You guys hosted a few quarterbacks, including Jaylen Daniels and Chandler Morris. What did you think about their play today? Not only how they improved and played, but how you could evaluate other players throughout the offense. >> I think that's the toughest position day one that you try to read and get a handle on because they have to learn so much. not just their job, but everybody else's job and get them lined up and audible. So, that's tough. He's very athletic. He's very bright. Love his attitude, both of them. Uh they know where to go with the ball. And as they get more comfortable, you'll start seeing them make more plays. But to say you get a whole bunch of install on day one as a quarterback, then go out and practice it with 11 new guys that you don't know to be on the same page. That's going to be a little different. >> What impresses you about Matt Harris? obviously played locally here at USF. >> Toughness, uh, leadership and toughness. He understands how to play the mic position. Uh, he's going to be very interesting. You know, if we can get to training camp and see him go from there with pads on, but he he's a leader. Uh, he understands the game very well and he'll be a good piece to see if he can move around and play special teams. for being to walk in here with a sap jersey on, paying homage to a fellow Kane and and a Buccaneer legend, >> but also just just some of the things that he said like your impressions of him as not just a player, but as a tone setter because because that's I mean he's coming in here, he's ultimately the one that that's the leader. >> He um you know, he got an old soul so to speak. He understands his lineage. He understands the guys that came before him. Uh they got a lot of great players down there at the University of Miami as well as the high schools down there as well. And he grew up around all those guys. Grew up around Bridgewater and Levante and Kansy and all those guys himself. So he understands tempo, he understands pace, he understands how to play hard, he understands to play homage to the guys that come before him that were down there and he tries to pattern his game like that. So he's a very smart player, not just a tough player. he understands what he's walking into and what he wants to be >> and and you've expressed multiple times this offseason your desire to have a certain type of of mentality on defense, guys with an edge. So, when you're you're doing your draft prep and you're looking at, you know, two guys from the same school, Miami, that helped take that program, you know, they they didn't ultimately accomplish what they wanted to at the end of the season, but to get to the national title game, like you have to have some some real difference makers, some some culture changers. like how important was that for you um to bring that to your football team? >> It was very important. You know, the one thing we wanted to do was get bigger. Number one, we thought we needed more size. I thought we were a little small last year. Me and Jason both thought that. Uh so to bring in two guys from the same school that happened to go to the national championship game. Uh I think Bane fell to us and luckily Kee fell to us. But there are a lot of teams that have those type of guys. Uh those type of guys that we had rated high when it was our turn to pick. So, it kind of fit what we were looking for. >> You guys come to the national national coaching academy this week. Um, you you've gotten to lead some sessions in that. Just want to ask you what you like about bringing young coaches in and and kind of just bringing the profession along with a week like this. >> You get a chance to see uh true emotion and feel and these guys really want to learn and you learn a lot from them because they're from all over the place and you know it's been tough on one of them this year cuz they got a little injured yesterday on their own going in motion. and we had an Achilles go. But you know that that's that's kind of tough. That's kind of tough right there. But they they come in and they're so eager to learn and they understand ball and to see them out there and it's only 32 jobs whether there's head or whether it's any other spot. But it gets you faces with names and it's great to know personalities before you know coaching pedigree because you can kind of see how they would coach if they fit in your system. So, you never know what may open up. It gives them a chance to see it firsthand. It gives us a chance to get to know them firsthand and how everything works. So, if something does open up and you can reach out and you can find somebody, it really helps both sides. >> We talked about this a little bit at the combine actually about like um you know, it's more of the interview process of interviewing guys that you've never worked with before or you haven't met before. But like for you as a coach where you have staff openings, you had staff openings this past year. How can hosting something like this every year allow you to expand your coaching tree or even have some of your your peers in the industry, you know, expanding their coaching trees because you can actually, you know, endorse that guy because you work with them. >> Well, like I tell them from the academy, it's not just getting to know me or knowing Jason. They're they're better off knowing the other coaches because they're a lot younger than I am, so they'll be in it a lot longer. So, you know, it's good to get to know everybody. Even if you coach DBs, you need to go meet the quarterback coach or the wide out coach needs to go see the Dline coach or the players so you can get to know them and get a feel for them and they can get a feel for you. And the more of us that have eyes on you and get you you get to sit in front of, the more we can compare notes and we can give you a better assessment of uh how we're doing if we need somebody. >> Thank you.

title: Nick Schrage on The National Coaching Academy Experience | Press Conference | Tampa Bay Buccaneers
text: Well, good afternoon, everybody. How we doing? Good. How are you? I'm well. I'm well. I'm happy to be here. Just talk about the experience, just kind of going through the process, submitting your application, getting the call. How how did all that come about? And what were the emotions along each step? Oh, gosh, sir. I I would say it's been it's been a whirlwind. You know, um the transition really from where I was at the College of William & Mary under Coach Mike London. Um and then transitioning to uh the current phase that I'm in as the assistant special teams and specialist coach at Rice. Uh I was recommended to apply here for the National Coaching Academy the for the third cohort. I mean, from what I've seen uh in person, it's it's as advertised. Made that application is it's rigorous. You get 90 seconds to uh debrief a play um and and really share your story uh amongst what I've now known is about a thousand applicants and to that I'm incredibly humbled. Uh and when that all came to pass, I I just got into Houston, right? Uh just 21-hour drive from Williamsburg all the way out to South Main and then I was during spring ball, got the the message and it was it was pretty quick, fast, and in a hurry because, you know, it hits your phone and then you look down and it's like, all right, I got to get out there. I got I got to walk out spring ball. So, it's been awesome. It's been a great experience. You guys have had a bunch of sessions with with Ken, Coach GM, some really big name former coaches. [cough] Uh what's have been the the coolest thing you've learned from those sessions so far? Uh I would just say that it's the it's the consistency and the level of professionalism, right? From from what I'm gathering from, you know, Coach Dungy, Coach Arians, um Jason Light, uh Coach Bowles, I mean, the the list goes on is that football is is not hard, gentlemen. It's it's about a game of consistency, right? The level of practice, preparation, um really the toughness and the expectation is is very high given, you know, this industry. And I would say that I'm able to piece together here in the National Football League that it's not about necessarily the X's and the O's. It's really about just coming in every day and maintaining that level of consistency um and then the coaches exemplify that daily. Coaching is is not just about skill, but it's also about your connections and and building connections with other people. So, like for you coming to something like this, um how does that allow you to expand your coaching tree? So, where if you're in a head coaching role one day, you can maybe have a greater pool of people to choose from. But also, if if someone you know, one of your contacts maybe even from here uh is assembling a staff, you could potentially be part of that. Oh, yes, ma'am. You know, um from the the very beginning, from when I was a player at Army West Point, Coach Jeff Monken and Sean Saucier um they did an exemplary job at explaining to us or really the importance of the network, right? And establishing authentic relationships. And I and I saw that when I transitioned out of the military after, you know, 6 years of service as a captain, uh the network really really showed its its teeth and what it what it meant to, you know, really branch out and get into a new industry. But being in here really just galvanized that. Um seeing everybody out here, you know, the expectations could be left or right of how an NFL coach could be or how players can be. But I mean, it's been nothing short of phenomenal. Um they've been pro- professional. Uh they guide you through it. Uh and it shows that down the line, it's not about, "Hey, can I get a job today?" Right? It's you're building an authentic relationship. You're asking the right questions. And I I mean, with with Coach P, it's been great. You know, he he's forgotten more football than I'll ever know. And asking him the questions and not being ashamed to do so, um you know, I feel a lot more comfortable in myself as a coach. You know, I I have a long ways to go before I get to don an NFL badge, but you know, I I'm grateful for the opportunity to be here today, you know, Coach Bowles, um Mr. Light, uh you know, the Glazer family, they're opening their doors to me is incredibly humbling. Can you talk about your transition from like your time in the military and then how you went from that to getting into coaching? Uh yes, ma'am. So, uh out of high school, let me make this brief, guys. Um I was a graduate of Fork Union Military Academy in Fork Union, Virginia. Um I did not get recruited out of high school, so I needed a post-graduate year. I was fortunate enough to be recruited by uh Jeff Monken and uh Sean Sestina at the Army and I jumped at that opportunity with open arms. Really I got to see how they did business over at West Point. I mean it's it's about toughness, humility, effort and execution and they're developing us to be leaders of character and leaders of men because the mission set for us really is to lead America's sons and daughters in the crucible of ground combat. That's a very specific and different mission and one that I'm incredibly honored to have had. Um went off, did my training, was an engineer officer, went to Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri. Uh my first duty station was at Fort Stewart in Savannah, Georgia and I'm there 3 months and I'm in uh in the Republic of Korea for 9 months. Uh we're at Camp Casey Hovey, come home, 6 months I'm up to platoon leader, first lieutenant at this point and Russia invades Ukraine as you all remember and I I we're over there in Eastern Europe and you know that again it it an immense honor to actually do the thing and and and to have served with such phenomenal men and women. You know, I I had my last go around and my last duty assignment in um Joint Base uh Myer Henderson Hall in DC where I started cutting my teeth in a coaching at the high school level um cuz I missed the game. Right? And when I transitioned out of the service I I still wanted to mentor young men and forge men because the game always mean nothing. Right? The game gave me everything. I'm first generation Brazilian to parents here from South Florida and so when my father died young the best men in my life were football coaches. Um and I saw that the resounding aspect was their character. And I wanted to give back. I couldn't sit behind the desk, you know, there's nothing wrong with it but I wanted to ensure that I was able to have a tangible hand in the next generation of young men to go out into the life to be better men, husbands and fathers. What are some of the things you're going to take and maybe implement yourself from from you know, this coaching experience that you that you're getting here? Oh, absolutely. No, so the biggest thing I'm seeing here is practice habits and professionalism. I mean, ladies and gentlemen, it it is a resounding echo when you go out to practice and you see the emphasis on the details. Right, and the players carry themselves with with that professionalism. I can't stop using that word because the pace of play, right, a running back's ability to angle step, go outside the the outside leg of the tackle, cut inside, and it's everybody. And it's an expectation, it's a standard that is undaunted. It's not tested. And the coaches, you know, it's it's a different level. These are are professional coaches with professional players, so it's like a pure sense of leadership. And they do a great job, and I'm I'm going to bring that back to the fore, you know, at Rice University. I'm I'm blessed to be here as an ambassador to Scott Abel's program. Um, and I'm ensuring that all the things that I have here, and I still have a few more days, God bless, um, are brought back, and I'm able to apply that into Scott Abel's second season over in South Main. It's unimaginable being in a conflict zone. Um, how has that shaped your perspective as a coach and as a leader? Well, ma'am, I'll say first and foremost, I was never in a combat zone, right? Uh, the Correcting. >> No, yes, ma'am. Um, but when we No, no, no, yes, ma'am. Um, Eastern Europe, you know, I was in Grafenwoehr, uh, over in Germany, and we went to Hohenfels, the JMRC, Joint Multinational Readiness Center, as we're operating with our NATO allies and cohort, as preparing for what we didn't know what the mission set it was at the time. Um, so we were just operating, you know, ready to, you know, engage and destroy the enemy in close quarters combat if need be, but, you know, those decisions were made by personnel at a higher level, a higher echelon than I. And, um, but the things that I was able to understand, I pulled from football, and I pulled from the roots at West Point. I I I can't begin to express, uh, my undying, uh, faith and appreciation for that academy, right? Coach Monk and the things I learned on the field, I was able to translate, uh, to my uh, to my soldiers, right? And when I was scared at times, and there were scary moments, and I was unsure, I always remembered, okay, if I could do this in front of 110,000 in Oklahoma, um, 2018 against Kyler Murray, and kick a football, and everyone's jaw not, I could do this, right? But it's ensuring to them that as long as long as I'm that steel rod and I'm undaunted, right? I'm okay. >> [snorts] >> Thank you. Thank you ladies and gentlemen so much.

title: Ted Hurst, Billy Schrauth and Bauer Sharp Discuss Rookie Minicamp
text: Congratulations on graduating by the way. >> Thank you. >> So, first workout out there, they thrown a lot at you obviously in these these mini camps. How do you think it went? And we saw you making some plays there, especially late in that day. >> Yeah, man. Um feel like coach coach BMAC is a great coach. He been staying on me, you know, he told me, you know, I have to get in shape coming in, you know, just running drills and running short routes and all of that. So, just kind of trying to prepare myself. >> How much have you been diving into the playbook since you arrived? >> Yeah, I've been diving into the playbook really hard, you know, looking over it at night, you know, getting that install, you know, trying to perfect that, you know, because that's a, you know, key aspect to you getting on the field and playing like I want to play early. >> What role are you primarily focusing on right now or are you cross training in and all the the roles. >> Um I I would say just getting better at every day every day working on my craft, you know, stay in that playbook. That's kind of what I'm looking forward to doing right now. >> I was going to say I know like with this with Zack with Zack Robinson, like traditionally that offense hasn't had like a true X receiver, but I know like also in past years we did see that a little bit more. So like for you, is there one particular spot that you feel like you're kind of honing in on a little bit or you kind of learn it all right now? >> X position for sure. you had a chance to meet any guys in the room, the veterans at all or >> Oh, yeah. Not not not yet. Um, I met Greeny though, but he was a pretty cool, you know, kind of advanced. He's helping me learn right now. the fact that like rookie receivers have had opportunities to make real impact the last two years whether it was Jaylen McMillan a couple years ago where you know seven touchdowns in the final five games led the league with that and then last last year Acha and Tz Johnson both like I mean does that does that excite you knowing that like you could have opportunities to get out there right away and do something for this team. Yeah, that's definitely motivation for me. You know, seeing a younger guy come in and, you know, step into that role and, you know, be a professional, also, you know, cause an impact on the game early. Yeah, that's motivation for me. >> You're going to get to work with Baker Mayfield this season and coming up soon. Just talk about your excitement level to to play with him. >> Yeah, man. You know, he's a great quarterback and I'm looking forward to that. You know, I'm I'm pretty sure he know how to make every throw. So, you know, just just learning from him, you know, him teaching me if he if I ever get the chance to, that that would be amazing. >> What do you think the biggest challenge is for you adjusting to the pro game, maybe adjusting to physicality or what is it that >> um I just say overall, you know, I've got a pretty feel good feel for the game. But I would just say becoming a pro and you know, how to go about things like the small things, the resources outside, you know, your nutrition, weight room, um recovery, all those small things. your story, no stars, you know, coming out of Georgia State, do you feel like you made it? Do you feel like you still got something to prove? Where's your mindset right now? >> Yeah, I definitely feel like, you know, I still got something to prove. There's a lot of doubters on, you know, my my potential and where I can go at, you know, in this profession. But, you know, I I you know, I have that talk with myself and it's kind of like, you know, um a little fuel to my fire. I see. >> You mentioned you could have gone, you know, left Georgia State, you decided to stay there, but then when you went to the Senior Bowl and got to compete against, you know, guys another level and you dominated, how much confidence did that give you and and and the ability to show scouts what you were capable of? >> Yeah. Yeah. I say I got, you know, great confidence, but I believe, you know, if I prepare myself the right way every time, it doesn't matter who I go against. You you mentioned talking to yourself like um I don't know if you're comfortable revealing this, but like what are some of those conversations you have? Like are we talking about like daily affirmations and things like that? >> Yeah. Yeah, definitely. Uh I start my morning off. I actually uh got this book. It's called One Minute with God. And I start my day off by reading that book and you know that's confidence and you know God is a big part of my life. So I I I use that to you know I say start my day. How how has uh how has that uh impacted your your football journey, >> man? Yeah, I've been lucky to, you know, not run into any crazy injuries, you know, it also gave me an opportunity for, you know, other people to look at me and, you know, just coming from where I come from. A lot of guys don't get that opportunity and he's just been amazing financially, helping me out and everything. I believe that that comes from God. >> How do you like Tampa so far? >> It's hot. It's hot. Georgia. >> Yeah, it's hot in Georgia. Yeah, it's a it's a little more hot out here though for sure. >> We get we do get a breeze though. Like I mean being not landlocked does allow some some breeze. What you really got to worry about is when those flags are not moving upstairs when they're stationary. >> Oh, >> it gets bad like in August and July. >> Yeah. They said around training camp it's going to get even crazier. >> You got time to acclimate them. It's a process. >> Said even yesterday like that's a big thing at the start of rookie man camp but seeing how guys adjust to the heat. You feel like you'll be able to handle that? >> Yeah. Yeah, I'll be all right. Just give me about a week. About a week, I'll be okay. >> If I remember correctly, you caught the last the last uh pass of of practice, I think yesterday. Like the importance for you because a lot of times, especially when you are physically fatigued, mental fatigue, like that's that's when you have to kind of look for for guys to maybe like, you know, do they have the same level of concentration? Then how important is it for you to finish practice on a high note? >> Yeah. Um, I kind of always tell myself, you know, my brother's really hard on me about what's my why. And, you know, when you get tired and fatigued, you know, think about that why and that reason that you're out here and just let that motivate you to go, you know, go hard when it when when you're tired at times. >> What is your why? >> Um, my why is shoot u uh I have a niece. My older brother had a had a daughter and you know he kind of paved the way for me in my profession and where I'm at today and and I got a younger brother and I feel like you know if he can use my name to open the door for him then you know that's amazing. >> Can you tell us a little bit more about your older brother? >> Yeah man, my brother is a kind of um you know my backbone, my right-hand man at the same time.
